sub: Web architecture, client-server communication, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS and hosting
q: An API endpoint has moved permanently to a new path. Clients POST JSON to the old path, and the server's redirect makes browsers re-issue the call as a GET with no body, so the write silently never happens. Which redirect status code should the server return so that clients repeat the request permanently at the new URL while keeping the POST method and the body?

opts.A: 301 Moved Permanently
opts.B: 303 See Other
opts.C: 308 Permanent Redirect
opts.D: 302 Found

exp: 308 is the only permanent redirect that forbids the user agent from changing the request method or dropping the body. 307 preserves the method too but signals a temporary move; 301 and 302 are the exact codes whose historical handling rewrites POST to GET, and 303 mandates that rewrite by definition.

sub: Web architecture, client-server communication, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS and hosting
q: A Python application is deployed behind Nginx acting as a reverse proxy on the same host. Its audit log, which records the requester's IP for every state-changing action, now shows 127.0.0.1 for every request. What is the correct fix?

opts.A: Have Nginx add the originating address in an X-Forwarded-For header and configure the application to read the client IP from that trusted header
opts.B: Add `proxy_set_header Host $host;` to the proxied location so the upstream sees the real hostname
opts.C: Disable `proxy_buffering` so Nginx streams the request straight through without rewriting it
opts.D: Bind the application to 0.0.0.0 instead of 127.0.0.1 so it receives connections directly

exp: A reverse proxy terminates the client's TCP connection and opens its own to the upstream, so the upstream legitimately sees the proxy's address; the original address survives only if the proxy forwards it in a header such as X-Forwarded-For and the app is told to trust that header from the proxy. Setting the Host header is a real and often necessary directive, but Host carries the requested site name, not the client address.

sub: Web architecture, client-server communication, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS and hosting
q: Nginx proxies to an application server with `proxy_read_timeout 60s;`. A report-generation request takes about 90 seconds to complete. The upstream is up and accepts the connection, but the browser gets an error page at the one-minute mark. Which status does Nginx return?

opts.A: 502 Bad Gateway
opts.B: 504 Gateway Timeout
opts.C: 503 Service Unavailable
opts.D: 408 Request Timeout

exp: When the upstream accepts the connection but sends nothing within proxy_read_timeout, Nginx gives up waiting and returns 504, the code reserved for a gateway that did not get a timely response from the server it depends on. 502 is what you would see if the upstream refused the connection or returned a malformed response, which is not the case here; 408 concerns a client that is slow to send its own request.

sub: Web architecture, client-server communication, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS and hosting
q: A department wants the bare domain `revenue.mizoram.in` to resolve to a cloud load balancer that is published only as a hostname, not as a fixed IP address. Adding a CNAME record at the zone apex is rejected. Why, and what is the standard remedy?

opts.A: CNAME records may not carry a TTL below 300 seconds; raise the TTL and the record will be accepted
opts.B: The apex may only hold records for subdomains; move the site to `www.revenue.mizoram.in` as the only possible option
opts.C: A DNAME record should be placed at the apex, since DNAME is the form of aliasing defined for a zone's own name
opts.D: A CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the same name, and the apex must hold SOA and NS records; DNS providers solve this with an ALIAS/ANAME-style record that resolves the target and answers with its A/AAAA addresses

exp: DNS forbids a CNAME alongside any other record at the same owner name, and every zone apex necessarily carries SOA and NS records, so an apex CNAME is invalid by construction; providers work around it with a synthetic ALIAS/ANAME record (also marketed as CNAME flattening) that follows the target and returns address records instead. DNAME is the tempting wrong answer: it aliases everything *below* a name, not the name itself, so it does not answer a query for the apex.

sub: Web architecture, client-server communication, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS and hosting
q: An administrator wants a single free Let's Encrypt certificate covering `*.mizoram.in`, because new subdomains are created for departments without notice. Which challenge type must be used to obtain it?

opts.A: HTTP-01, by serving a token file under /.well-known/acme-challenge/ on each host
opts.B: DNS-01, by publishing the required TXT record under _acme-challenge in the zone
opts.C: TLS-ALPN-01, by presenting the validation certificate during the TLS handshake on port 443
opts.D: Any of the challenge types; wildcard issuance only requires that the account has already validated the base domain

exp: Let's Encrypt issues wildcard certificates only against DNS-01 validation, because control of an individual web server proves nothing about the arbitrary subdomains a wildcard would cover, whereas writing a TXT record proves control of the zone itself. HTTP-01 is the everyday default for ordinary hostnames and is the most tempting choice here, but it is explicitly not accepted for wildcard names.

sub: Web architecture, client-server communication, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS and hosting
q: HTTP/2 already multiplexes many concurrent streams over one connection, yet on a lossy mobile link a single dropped packet still stalls every stream in flight. Which property of HTTP/3 addresses this?

opts.A: It runs over QUIC on UDP, where loss recovery is per-stream, so a lost packet delays only the stream whose data it carried
opts.B: It compresses headers, so fewer packets are sent and the chance of loss is correspondingly reduced
opts.C: It opens a separate TCP connection per stream, restoring the parallelism that HTTP/1.1 clients got from multiple connections
opts.D: It makes encryption mandatory, so retransmissions are handled inside the TLS record layer rather than by the transport

exp: HTTP/2 removed head-of-line blocking at the application layer but still rides a single TCP connection, whose in-order delivery guarantee holds back every multiplexed stream until the missing segment is retransmitted; QUIC keeps streams independent at the transport layer, so only the affected stream waits. Header compression is real in both HTTP/2 (HPACK) and HTTP/3 (QPACK) but does nothing about ordering, and HTTP/3 uses fewer connections, not one per stream.

sub: Web architecture, client-server communication, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS and hosting
q: A site responds over HTTPS with `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`. A user who visited the site yesterday now types `http://site.gov.in/login` into the same browser. What does a compliant browser do?

opts.A: Sends the plaintext HTTP request as typed, then follows the server's 301 redirect to the HTTPS URL
opts.B: Sends the request over HTTP but adds an Upgrade-Insecure-Requests header asking the server to switch
opts.C: Rewrites the URL to https:// internally and makes no cleartext request to the site at all
opts.D: Refuses to load the page and shows a certificate error until the user types the https:// form explicitly

exp: While a host's HSTS policy is still within max-age, the browser upgrades any http:// URL for that host to https:// before opening a connection, which is precisely what removes the one cleartext round trip an on-path downgrade attack needs. Option A describes the pre-HSTS behaviour that a plain redirect gives you, and it is the tempting answer because the server usually still sends that redirect — the browser just never reaches it.

sub: HTML, semantic elements, forms, multimedia, Canvas, SVG and accessibility
q: A developer nests an <h1> inside a <section> that is itself inside another <section>, expecting assistive technology to announce it as a third-level heading. What actually happens in current browsers and screen readers?

opts.A: It is announced as a level 1 heading; the sectioning-based outline algorithm was never implemented by browsers and has been dropped from the HTML standard
opts.B: It is announced as a level 3 heading, matching the depth of <section> nesting
opts.C: It is announced as a level 2 heading, because a sectioning element demotes its heading by exactly one level however deeply it is nested
opts.D: It is announced as a heading of undefined level, leaving assistive technology to infer structure from document order

exp: Heading level is taken from the tag name alone: <h1> is level 1 no matter how many sectioning ancestors wrap it, because the proposed document outline algorithm shipped in no engine and was removed from the spec. The level-3 option describes the behaviour the algorithm was supposed to produce, which is exactly why the myth persists; author the correct <h2>/<h3> explicitly.

sub: HTML, semantic elements, forms, multimedia, Canvas, SVG and accessibility
q: A page has a site-wide menu and a breadcrumb trail, each in its own <nav> element. A screen-reader user opening the landmarks list hears "navigation" twice with nothing to distinguish them. What is the correct fix?

opts.A: Give each <nav> a unique id, which assistive technology exposes as the landmark's accessible name
opts.B: Put aria-hidden="true" on the breadcrumb <nav> so only one navigation landmark is announced
opts.C: Give each <nav> a distinct accessible name with aria-label or aria-labelledby
opts.D: Replace the breadcrumb <nav> with <div role="navigation">, which does not create a duplicate landmark entry

exp: Repeated landmarks of the same type are disambiguated by giving each one an accessible name, which for a <nav> comes from aria-label or aria-labelledby. The <div role="navigation"> option changes nothing, since an explicit role and its native element expose the identical landmark; and aria-hidden would remove the breadcrumbs from the accessibility tree entirely rather than label them.

sub: HTML, semantic elements, forms, multimedia, Canvas, SVG and accessibility
q: A checkout form contains <input name="coupon" value="FEST26" disabled>. The user presses the submit button. What does the server receive for coupon?

opts.A: coupon=FEST26, because the value attribute is present regardless of the control's state
opts.B: Nothing at all — a disabled control is not successful, so no name/value pair is sent for it
opts.C: coupon= with an empty value
opts.D: Nothing, and the browser additionally blocks the submission with a constraint-validation error

exp: Disabled controls are excluded from the form's entry list, so the key is simply absent from the payload — not present-and-empty, which is what readonly would give you (readonly controls are submitted with their value). Nothing about disabled participates in constraint validation either, so the submission itself proceeds normally.

sub: HTML, semantic elements, forms, multimedia, Canvas, SVG and accessibility
q: Five radio buttons ask the candidate to choose a preferred exam centre. Each <input> has its own correctly associated <label>, but a screen-reader user hears only the individual centre names and never the question itself. Which markup supplies the group's accessible name?

opts.A: Wrap the radios in a <fieldset> whose <legend> contains the question text
opts.B: Wrap all five inputs in one <label> element that also contains the question text
opts.C: Place an <h3> containing the question immediately before the radio buttons
opts.D: Put title="Preferred exam centre" on the <div> that contains the radios

exp: <fieldset> groups related controls and its <legend> becomes the group's accessible name, so each radio is announced together with the question. A preceding <h3> is the most tempting alternative because it looks right on screen, but a heading is not programmatically associated with the controls; and a plain <div> has no role, so a title on it exposes no name.

sub: HTML, semantic elements, forms, multimedia, Canvas, SVG and accessibility
q: A landing page uses <video src="promo.mp4" autoplay> with an ordinary audio track. On desktop Chrome the video sits on its first frame and never starts; the only sign of trouble is a rejected play() promise. What explains this?

opts.A: The autoplay attribute has no effect unless preload="auto" is also set
opts.B: A <video> element will not start automatically unless the controls attribute is present
opts.C: The src attribute is ignored on <video>; media must be supplied through child <source> elements
opts.D: Browser autoplay policy blocks unmuted autoplay without a user gesture; adding muted (with playsinline for mobile) lets it start

exp: Chrome and the other major engines permit autoplay only when the media is muted or the user has already interacted with the origin, and a blocked attempt surfaces as a rejected play() promise exactly as described. The preload option is a red herring — preload governs buffering, not permission to play — and <video> accepts src directly, with <source> only needed for multiple formats.

sub: HTML, semantic elements, forms, multimedia, Canvas, SVG and accessibility
q: A recorded training video already ships a <track> with kind="subtitles" carrying a translation of the dialogue. An accessibility audit still records a failure for deaf and hard-of-hearing users. Which track kind must be added?

opts.A: kind="descriptions", which narrates what is happening on screen
opts.B: kind="captions", which carries the dialogue plus speaker identification and relevant non-speech sound
opts.C: kind="chapters", which exposes navigable sections of the timeline
opts.D: kind="metadata", which carries cue data for scripts to consume

exp: Subtitles assume the viewer can hear and only render the spoken words, whereas captions are written for a viewer who hears nothing and must therefore also convey speaker changes and meaningful non-speech audio. The descriptions option is a genuine track kind but solves the opposite problem — it serves blind users by narrating the visuals.

sub: HTML, semantic elements, forms, multimedia, Canvas, SVG and accessibility
q: An interactive seat-selection map is drawn entirely with the Canvas 2D API, and clicks are resolved from pointer coordinates against an internal seat array. Screen-reader users perceive nothing on the page. Which approach fixes this using the mechanism Canvas itself provides?

opts.A: Add an alt attribute to the <canvas> element describing the seating layout
opts.B: Set aria-live="polite" on the <canvas> so each drawing operation is announced as it occurs
opts.C: Place focusable, labelled DOM elements — one per seat — inside the <canvas> element as its fallback content, and keep them in sync with what is drawn
opts.D: Supply a <noscript> block containing an accessible seat list

exp: Child content of <canvas> is the spec's designated fallback and shadow DOM for the bitmap: it is exposed to assistive technology and can be focused and activated, so mirroring each seat as a real button gives keyboard and screen-reader access to the same interaction. aria-live is the seductive wrong answer — drawing to a canvas mutates a bitmap, not the DOM, so there is no mutation for a live region to announce, and <noscript> never renders for a screen-reader user with JavaScript enabled.

sub: HTML, semantic elements, forms, multimedia, Canvas, SVG and accessibility
q: An icon exists as an .svg file. The team needs it to take its fill from the page's currentColor and to change colour on hover through an ordinary CSS rule. This works when the . Why?

opts.A: rasterises the SVG at load time, discarding the vector paths that CSS would target
opts.B: SVG elements obey only presentation attributes such as fill; CSS declarations never apply to them
opts.C: currentColor is a CSS-only keyword with no meaning inside SVG, so only literal colour values work there
opts.D: An SVG loaded through is an isolated document — the page's CSS and scripts cannot reach its elements, and inherited values such as currentColor do not cross that boundary

exp: Referencing an SVG from renders it as an independent, non-scriptable document, so page stylesheets never match its shapes and it has no parent from which to inherit currentColor; inlining puts the same shapes in the page's own DOM where both apply. The rasterisation option is wrong on its own terms — the image still scales as a vector, it is simply unreachable from outside.

sub: HTML, semantic elements, forms, multimedia, Canvas, SVG and accessibility
q: GIGW 3.0, the Guidelines for Indian Government Websites issued under MeitY, requires government websites and mobile apps to conform to WCAG 2.1 at which conformance level?

opts.A: Level A
opts.B: Level AA
opts.C: Level AAA
opts.D: WCAG 2.1 defines no conformance levels; GIGW substitutes its own percentage compliance score

exp: GIGW 3.0 sets Level AA of WCAG 2.1 as the accessibility bar for Indian government web properties, matching the level used in public-procurement accessibility requirements internationally. Level AAA is not the answer anywhere — WCAG itself advises against requiring full AAA conformance for entire sites, since some AAA criteria cannot be met for all content types.

sub: CSS, Flexbox, Grid and responsive web design
q: A flex row contains an item holding a long unbroken log line. The item refuses to shrink and pushes the row wider than its container, even though flex-shrink is at its default of 1. Which declaration on that flex item resolves the overflow?

opts.A: flex-shrink: 2
opts.B: min-width: 0
opts.C: max-width: 100%
opts.D: flex-basis: 0

exp: A flex item's initial min-width is auto, which floors its used width at its min-content size, so shrinking stops there; min-width: 0 removes that floor. flex-shrink: 2 changes nothing because the item is already being asked to shrink and is blocked by the automatic minimum, and max-width cannot help because the minimum size wins over the maximum when the two conflict.

sub: CSS, Flexbox, Grid and responsive web design
q: In a display: flex navigation row, the final link must sit hard against the right edge while the remaining links stay grouped at the left. No spacer element may be added and justify-content must stay at its default. Which declaration on the last item achieves this?

opts.A: align-self: flex-end
opts.B: justify-self: end
opts.C: margin-left: auto
opts.D: float: right

exp: An auto margin on a flex item absorbs all free space on that side before justify-content is applied, so margin-left: auto pushes the item to the far end of the main axis. align-self only moves the item on the cross axis, justify-self is ignored in flex layout entirely, and float has no effect because a flex container ignores float and clear on its items: they neither float nor are taken out of flow. Blockification is a separate rule — it changes a flex item's display value — and it is not what disables the float.
reviewFix: Explanation fixed. The key (margin-left: auto) and the other rebuttals were correct, but the float rebuttal gave a false mechanism: 'float has no effect on a flex item because floating is blockified away during flex item creation'. css-flexbox-1 treats these as two separate rules — a flex item's display value is blockified, and separately float and clear do not create floating or clearance for flex items and do not take them out of flow. Float is not blockified away; it is ignored while remaining a specified value. The wording also inverted the normal-flow rule, where float is what causes blockification. Key unchanged.

sub: CSS, Flexbox, Grid and responsive web design
q: A CSS Grid gallery mixes single-column items with items that span two columns, and is declared grid-auto-flow: row dense. Compared with plain grid-auto-flow: row, what does the dense keyword change?

opts.A: It reduces the gap between tracks so items pack together with no leftover space
opts.B: It forces all auto-placed items onto one row, creating implicit columns as needed
opts.C: It makes every implicitly created row take the height of the tallest item in the grid
opts.D: It lets the placement algorithm go back and fill earlier holes with later items that fit, so visual order can diverge from DOM order

exp: Sparse (default) placement never moves the cursor backwards, so a wide item that does not fit leaves a hole; dense placement revisits those holes with any later item small enough to fit, which is why it can reorder content visually and is an accessibility concern for keyboard and screen-reader order. Gap size is controlled by the gap property and is untouched by grid-auto-flow.

sub: CSS, Flexbox, Grid and responsive web design
q: A hero image must be a wide landscape crop on desktop and a genuinely different, tighter portrait crop on phones — two separate files, not two sizes of one file. Which approach lets the browser fetch only the crop it will actually display?

opts.A: A single whose srcset lists both files with w descriptors and a matching sizes attribute
opts.B: A element with a pointing at the portrait crop and an fallback carrying the landscape crop
opts.C: A single whose srcset lists both files with x descriptors for 1x and 2x
opts.D: Two elements, with the unwanted one hidden via display: none inside a media query

exp: This is art direction rather than resolution switching: evaluates each media condition in order and loads only the first match, so the crop is chosen deterministically by viewport. The srcset options are wrong because w and x descriptors are hints for resolution switching and the browser is free to pick either candidate regardless of viewport shape, and display: none does not reliably prevent an from being fetched.

sub: CSS, Flexbox, Grid and responsive web design
q: A design system wraps its base selectors in :where(...) so that page-level CSS can override them without specificity fights. Compared with :is(...), what does :where() do differently?

opts.A: :where() always contributes zero specificity, while :is() takes the specificity of its most specific argument
opts.B: :where() matches only the first selector in its list, while :is() matches any of them
opts.C: :where() pierces shadow DOM boundaries, while :is() is confined to the current tree
opts.D: :where() may appear only at the start of a compound selector, while :is() may appear anywhere in it

exp: The two pseudo-classes match identically; the sole difference is specificity, with :where() contributing nothing and :is() adopting the weight of its heaviest argument. That is exactly why a reset written as :where(.card) h2 is overridable by a later single-class rule, whereas :is(.card) h2 would still carry class-level weight.

sub: CSS, Flexbox, Grid and responsive web design
q: A card component appears both in a wide main column and in a narrow sidebar on the same page at the same viewport width, and must switch to its stacked layout only when it is in the sidebar. Which CSS mechanism expresses this?

opts.A: @media (max-width: 400px), because media query lengths resolve against the nearest block container
opts.B: @supports (inline-size: 400px), which tests the element's own box against the given size
opts.C: @container after declaring container-type: inline-size on the card's wrapper, because media queries only ever resolve against the viewport
opts.D: @media (min-width: 400px) placed in the sidebar's own stylesheet, since media queries are scoped to the stylesheet that declares them

exp: Media queries have exactly one subject, the viewport (or print surface), so they cannot distinguish two instances of a component that share a viewport; container queries evaluate against a named ancestor that has opted in via container-type, making the component responsive to its own available inline size. @supports is a feature query that tests declaration support, not element dimensions.

sub: CSS, Flexbox, Grid and responsive web design
q: A section heading is styled position: sticky; top: 0 and the browser supports sticky positioning, yet the heading scrolls away with the content instead of pinning. What is the most likely cause?

opts.A: An ancestor of the heading has overflow set to hidden, auto or scroll, so the heading sticks within that ancestor's scrollport rather than within the page
opts.B: position: sticky requires an explicit height on the sticky element itself
opts.C: position: sticky requires the parent to be position: relative to establish a containing block
opts.D: top: 0 is ignored on a sticky element unless z-index is set to auto

exp: A sticky element is positioned relative to its nearest scrolling ancestor, and any ancestor with a non-visible overflow value becomes that scroll container; if that container does not itself scroll, the element appears never to stick even though the CSS is valid. Option C is the familiar rule for position: absolute and does not apply here — sticky needs no positioned ancestor.

sub: CSS, Flexbox, Grid and responsive web design
q: A full-screen hero uses height: 100vh. On mobile browsers with a retracting URL bar the hero is taller than the visible area while the bar is shown. Which unit sizes the hero to the viewport as it currently is, growing and shrinking as the browser chrome retracts and returns?

opts.A: 100svh
opts.B: 100lvh
opts.C: 100vmin
opts.D: 100dvh

exp: The dynamic viewport unit dvh tracks the viewport as browser chrome expands and collapses, which is precisely the behaviour asked for. svh and lvh are the tempting near-misses: both are stable values, svh assuming the chrome is always shown and lvh assuming it is always retracted, and lvh is what 100vh effectively resolves to on those browsers in the first place.

sub: CSS, Flexbox, Grid and responsive web design
q: A heading is declared font-size: clamp(1rem, 4vw, 2rem). The root font size is the default 16px and the viewport width resolves to 1200px. What computed font size results?

opts.A: 16px
opts.B: 24px
opts.C: 32px
opts.D: 48px

exp: The preferred value 4vw evaluates to 48px at a 1200px viewport, which exceeds the maximum, so clamp() returns the maximum of 2rem = 32px. 48px is the trap for reading the middle argument as the result without applying the upper bound; note also that vw is a fraction of viewport width and is unaffected by the root font size.

sub: JavaScript, the DOM, event handling, asynchronous programming, JSON and Fetch
q: What is the return value of JSON.stringify([1, undefined, function () {}, 4]) ?

opts.B: '[1,undefined,undefined,4]'
opts.C: '[1,null,null,4]'
opts.D: It throws a TypeError, because a function is not serialisable

exp: When JSON.stringify meets undefined, a function or a symbol it omits the property if it is inside an object, but censors it to null inside an array, because an array element cannot simply vanish without shifting the indices. '[1,4]' is the behaviour you would get for object properties, not array elements, and nothing here throws.

sub: JavaScript, the DOM, event handling, asynchronous programming, JSON and Fetch
q: A page served from https://app.example.gov.in calls fetch('https://api.example.gov.in/profile'). The API already responds with Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to the exact app origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, yet the browser still sends no session cookie. Which change to the fetch call is required?

opts.A: Add credentials: 'include' to the request options
opts.B: Add mode: 'cors' to the request options
opts.C: Add mode: 'no-cors' to the request options
opts.D: Attach the session cookie yourself through the headers option

exp: fetch defaults to credentials: 'same-origin', so cookies are withheld on a cross-origin request until the caller opts in with 'include'; the server-side CORS headers are already in place here. mode: 'cors' is already the default for a cross-origin request and changes nothing, and Cookie is a forbidden header name that script cannot set.

sub: JavaScript, the DOM, event handling, asynchronous programming, JSON and Fetch

opts.A: Logs 'all saved' only after every save() has resolved
opts.B: Logs 'all saved' before any save() has resolved
opts.C: Throws a TypeError, because forEach does not accept an async callback
opts.D: Runs the saves strictly one after another, then logs 'all saved'

exp: forEach discards whatever its callback returns, so the promise from each async callback is thrown away; each callback runs synchronously only as far as its first await, and then forEach returns and the log executes before any continuation resumes. Sequential execution (option D) is what for...of with await would give you; Promise.all(items.map(save)) gives the concurrent wait.

sub: JavaScript, the DOM, event handling, asynchronous programming, JSON and Fetch
q: A submit listener added to a form with addEventListener logs its message and calls event.stopPropagation(), but the browser still submits the form and reloads the page. Why?

opts.A: stopPropagation() takes effect only on listeners registered for the capture phase
opts.B: The listener must be registered with { passive: false } before cancellation can take effect
opts.C: The handler must return false; addEventListener treats a false return value as a cancellation
opts.D: stopPropagation() only halts further propagation of the event; suppressing the browser's default submit needs preventDefault()

exp: Propagation and default action are two independent things: stopPropagation() keeps other listeners on ancestors from firing, while only preventDefault() cancels the navigation. Returning false cancels the default in inline handlers and in jQuery, but a return value from an addEventListener callback is ignored, and { passive: false } merely restores the ability to call preventDefault on scroll-blocking events such as touchstart and wheel.

sub: JavaScript, the DOM, event handling, asynchronous programming, JSON and Fetch
q: A dashboard issues six independent fetch calls and must render every panel whose call succeeded while marking the ones that failed, so a single rejection must not discard the other five results. Which promise combinator fits?

opts.A: Promise.all
opts.B: Promise.allSettled
opts.C: Promise.any
opts.D: Promise.race

exp: Promise.allSettled waits for every input promise and resolves with an array of {status, value} or {status, reason} objects, which is exactly the successes-plus-failures shape needed. Promise.all short-circuits on the first rejection and throws the other results away, while Promise.any resolves with only the first fulfilment.

sub: JavaScript, the DOM, event handling, asynchronous programming, JSON and Fetch
q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an element's textContent from its innerText?

opts.A: textContent returns the text of every descendant node, including ones hidden by CSS, whereas innerText approximates the rendered text and leaves them out
opts.B: Assigning a string to textContent parses it as HTML, whereas assigning to innerText does not
opts.C: innerText is read-only, whereas textContent can be both read and written
opts.D: Reading textContent forces a layout reflow, whereas reading innerText does not

exp: innerText is layout-aware, so it reflects what a user would actually see and skips subtrees hidden with display:none, while textContent walks the DOM and concatenates all text nodes regardless of styling. Option D is the truth reversed, since it is innerText that can trigger a reflow; neither property parses HTML on assignment, and both are writable.

sub: JavaScript, the DOM, event handling, asynchronous programming, JSON and Fetch
q: A type-ahead search box fires a fetch on every keystroke, and a stale response sometimes overwrites a newer one. The requirement is to actually cancel the earlier in-flight request when the next keystroke arrives. What does that?

opts.A: Call Promise.reject() inside the new keystroke handler to reject the earlier promise
opts.B: Call .cancel() on the promise object that the earlier fetch() returned
opts.C: Pass an AbortController's signal into fetch() and call controller.abort() on the next keystroke
opts.D: Set keepalive: false on the earlier request so the browser drops it

exp: AbortController is the standard cancellation channel for fetch: the request aborts and its promise rejects with an AbortError DOMException you can filter out in the catch block. Promises have no .cancel() method and cannot be rejected from outside, and keepalive only controls whether a request may outlive the page.

sub: JavaScript, the DOM, event handling, asynchronous programming, JSON and Fetch
q: An external script tag inside <head> runs document.querySelector('#app') and gets null, although that element exists in the body markup. Without moving the tag or wrapping the code in a DOMContentLoaded listener, which attribute fixes it while still guaranteeing this script runs before another external script tag that follows it in the document and carries the same attribute?

opts.A: async
opts.B: nomodule
opts.C: crossorigin="anonymous"
opts.D: defer

exp: defer downloads the script in parallel but delays execution until the document has been parsed, and deferred scripts run in document order, so both requirements are met. That ordering guarantee holds among deferred scripts only: a later plain classic script carries no defer or async, is parser-blocking, and would still run first — which is why the stem pins the following script to the same attribute. async also defers download but executes as soon as the file arrives, which may be before parsing finishes and in an order that depends on network timing.
reviewFix: Flagged by both blind passes as resting on an unstated assumption, and they were right. defer guarantees document order only against OTHER deferred scripts; if the following external script were a plain classic script it would be parser-blocking and execute BEFORE the deferred one, inverting the ordering the stem claimed to guarantee. As literally written no option satisfied the second requirement, and a student could have generalised that defer orders a script ahead of any later tag. sub: JavaScript, the DOM, event handling, asynchronous programming, JSON and Fetch

opts.B: json() resolves with null once text() has already been called
opts.C: json() rejects with a TypeError, because the response body stream has already been consumed

sub: Frontend frameworks: components, routing, state management and API integration
q: A React list is rendered as `items.map((item, i) => <Row key={i} item={item} />)`, and each `Row` holds its own local expanded/collapsed state. An item is then deleted from the middle of the array. What is the most likely visible bug?

opts.A: React logs a duplicate-key warning and refuses to render the rows after the deleted one
opts.B: Every row unmounts and remounts, so all rows reset to collapsed
opts.C: The expanded/collapsed state stays attached to list positions, so rows that shifted up now show the state that belonged to the row previously at that index
opts.D: The list stops re-rendering until the parent component is remounted

exp: With the array index as the key, reconciliation matches a component to a position rather than to an item, so deleting from the middle leaves each surviving row inheriting the local state of whatever previously sat at its new index. Full unmount-and-remount of every row is what a stable unique key would avoid, not what an index key causes — index keys make React reuse instances, which is exactly the problem.

sub: Frontend frameworks: components, routing, state management and API integration
q: A React component holds `const [items, setItems] = useState([])`. Its add handler runs `items.push(newItem); setItems(items);`. What happens when the handler fires?

opts.A: React throws an error because component state was mutated directly
opts.B: The UI does not update, because setItems receives the same array reference and React bails out of the re-render
opts.C: The component re-renders, but the newly pushed item is missing from the output
opts.D: The component re-renders twice, briefly showing the new item duplicated

exp: React compares the next state to the current one with Object.is, and a mutated-then-reassigned array is the same reference, so the update is skipped and the pushed item never appears; passing a new array such as `setItems([...items, newItem])` is the fix. React does not throw on direct mutation — it simply cannot detect the change, which is why the failure is silent rather than an error.

sub: Frontend frameworks: components, routing, state management and API integration
q: A dashboard has a persistent sidebar and header, while three sub-pages swap in and out of the content area as the URL changes. The sidebar must not re-mount or lose its scroll position during those swaps. Which client-side router feature describes this?

opts.A: Nested routes, where the child route renders into an outlet placed inside the parent route's component so the parent stays mounted
opts.B: Hash-based routing, which keeps the layout portion out of the URL path
opts.C: Route guards, which block navigation until the surrounding layout has finished loading
opts.D: Programmatic navigation, pushing each sub-page URL onto the history stack from an event handler

exp: Nested routing lets a parent route own persistent chrome and designate an outlet slot into which the matched child route renders, so only the child subtree changes on navigation. Programmatic navigation only chooses when to navigate; it says nothing about which parts of the tree survive the navigation.

sub: Frontend frameworks: components, routing, state management and API integration
q: An SPA uses a client-side route guard that redirects non-admin users away from /admin. A tester with an ordinary account opens devtools, calls GET /api/admin/users directly and receives the full data. What does this demonstrate?

opts.A: The guard was registered on the parent route only and must be repeated on every child route
opts.B: The access token should be stored in an httpOnly cookie instead of localStorage
opts.C: The admin screens should be moved into a lazy-loaded chunk so non-admins never download that code
opts.D: Route guards only decide what the SPA renders; authorization must be enforced by the server on every API request

exp: Everything a browser client does is under the user's control, so a guard is a navigation convenience and the API is the only place an access decision can actually be enforced. Lazy-loading the admin chunk is reasonable hygiene but changes nothing here — the endpoint was called directly, without loading any of the app's admin code.

sub: Frontend frameworks: components, routing, state management and API integration
q: A Vite-built SPA keeps a third-party API key in `.env` as `VITE_API_KEY`, reads it via `import.meta.env.VITE_API_KEY`, and calls the third-party API straight from the browser. The `.env` file is gitignored. Why is the key still exposed?

opts.A: The `.env` file is copied into the `dist/` output and served as a static asset
opts.B: Vite substitutes the literal value into the JavaScript bundle at build time, so it ships to every visitor and is readable in devtools
opts.C: `import.meta.env` is resolved by an HTTP request to the origin server on page load, exposing the value in the network tab
opts.D: The value is only exposed if source maps are deployed alongside the production bundle

exp: Vite performs a static text replacement of `import.meta.env.VITE_*` during the build, so the secret becomes a string literal inside the shipped JavaScript regardless of how the `.env` file is handled in version control; a browser-callable secret must instead be proxied through a backend. Source maps are irrelevant — the literal is present in the minified bundle whether or not maps are published.

sub: Frontend frameworks: components, routing, state management and API integration
q: In an SPA, most navigation uses the router's link component, but one menu entry was written as a plain `<a href='/reports'>`. Clicking it reaches the right page, yet the page visibly reloads and the app's in-memory store is empty afterwards. Why?

opts.A: The anchor is missing the router's configured base path, so the client router cannot match it against its route table
opts.B: The web server has no history fallback rule, so it re-serves index.html from cache instead of the route
opts.C: A plain anchor performs a full document navigation, so the browser tears down the running JavaScript context and boots a fresh app instance, discarding in-memory state
opts.D: The router intercepts clicks only on elements rendered inside its outlet, so the anchor must be moved inside the outlet

exp: Router link components exist precisely to intercept the click and call the History API instead of letting the browser navigate, which is what preserves the running app and its store. A missing history fallback would produce a 404 on reload, not a successful-but-full reload, so it does not explain this symptom.

sub: Frontend frameworks: components, routing, state management and API integration
q: A team already runs a global client-state store (Redux, Pinia or NgRx) and additionally adopts a dedicated server-state library such as TanStack Query for its REST calls. What does the server-state library primarily add?

opts.A: Caching keyed by request, deduplication of in-flight identical requests, staleness tracking and background refetching for data the server owns
opts.B: A single immutable state tree that makes UI state transitions predictable and replayable
opts.C: Enforcement of one-way data flow from parent components down to child components
opts.D: Persistence of the entire application state to localStorage so it survives a page reload

exp: Remote data is a cache of something another system owns, so it needs cache keys, invalidation, deduplication and refetch-on-stale — concerns a general-purpose store does not model. A single predictable state tree is what the store already provides, so it cannot be what the second library is being added for.

sub: Frontend frameworks: components, routing, state management and API integration
q: A task list flips a to-do's `completed` flag in local state immediately and fires the PATCH afterwards, so the checkbox responds instantly. Beyond applying the change early, what must this optimistic-update pattern also implement to remain correct?

opts.A: A debounce, so rapid repeated toggles collapse into a single request
opts.B: A longer request timeout, so the PATCH still completes on slow connections
opts.C: Polling the server every few seconds to re-synchronise the list
opts.D: A rollback that restores the previous value, and surfaces the failure, if the request is rejected

exp: An optimistic update asserts a server outcome before it is known, so the pattern is only sound if the pre-update snapshot is retained and reapplied when the request fails, otherwise the UI silently diverges from the database. Debouncing is a request-volume optimisation and does nothing about a rejected write.

sub: Frontend frameworks: components, routing, state management and API integration
q: A React app renders `<AuthContext.Provider value={{ user, setUser }}>` high in the tree. Profiling shows that every consumer of that context re-renders whenever the provider's own component re-renders, even when `user` is unchanged. What explains this?

opts.A: Context providers re-run all consumers on every render by design; the provider value is never compared
opts.B: Consumers must be wrapped in `React.memo` to skip re-renders caused by context
opts.C: The inline object literal produces a new value reference on each render, and consumers re-render when the provider value is not referentially equal to the previous one
opts.D: `setUser` must be excluded from the context value, because function identities are never stable across renders

exp: React compares the provider's value by reference, and `{{ user, setUser }}` allocates a fresh object each render, so memoising the value (for example with useMemo) is what stops the cascade. React.memo is the tempting wrong answer: it compares props and does not prevent a context update from re-rendering a consumer.

sub: Backend development in PHP and Python: REST APIs, CRUD, middleware, auth, sessions and ORM
q: A POST to /api/v1/orders succeeds and a new order resource now exists at its own URI. Which status code and response header pairing is the conventional REST result for this?

opts.A: 200 OK, with a Content-Location header naming the new order
opts.B: 202 Accepted, with a Retry-After header telling the client when to look again
opts.C: 201 Created, with a Location header naming the new order
opts.D: 204 No Content, with an ETag header for the new order

exp: A resource that has been created is reported with 201 Created, and the URI of the thing just created is advertised in the Location header. 202 Accepted is the tempting alternative but it means the work was only queued and no resource necessarily exists yet, which contradicts a stem that says the order was created.

sub: Backend development in PHP and Python: REST APIs, CRUD, middleware, auth, sessions and ORM
q: A Django project served by Gunicorn's default synchronous workers must add a WebSocket endpoint for live order tracking. Why can this deployment not host that endpoint as it stands?

opts.A: Synchronous Gunicorn workers cannot terminate TLS, and WebSocket endpoints must be served over TLS
opts.B: WSGI models a request as a single call in and a single response out, with no representation for a long-lived bidirectional connection, so an ASGI server is required instead
opts.C: Django's ORM is synchronous, so a WebSocket handler would be unable to query the database at all
opts.D: WebSockets are carried over HTTP/2 streams, which synchronous Gunicorn workers do not implement

exp: WSGI's contract is one callable invoked per request that returns one response body, which leaves no place for a connection that stays open and carries frames in both directions; ASGI was defined precisely to add that, and is what servers such as Uvicorn or Daphne speak. Option D is the plausible-sounding trap: the WebSocket handshake is an HTTP/1.1 Upgrade and does not depend on HTTP/2.

opts.A: $_SESSION is now empty and the application must write user_id again under the new identifier
opts.B: The session identifier is unchanged; only the session cookie's expiry time has been refreshed
opts.C: $_SESSION still holds user_id 42 under a new identifier, and the old session's data remains valid server-side until garbage collection removes it
opts.D: $_SESSION still holds user_id 42 under a newly issued identifier, and the old session's server-side data has been deleted

exp: session_regenerate_id() carries the current $_SESSION contents across to a freshly issued identifier, and its boolean argument controls whether the old session's server-side data is destroyed; passing true destroys it. Option C is exactly what happens when the argument is false or omitted, which is why the defence against session fixation is to regenerate with deletion at the moment privilege changes.

sub: Backend development in PHP and Python: REST APIs, CRUD, middleware, auth, sessions and ORM
q: An API endpoint requires a write scope. A request arrives bearing an OAuth 2.0 access token that is well-formed, correctly signed and unexpired, but whose granted scopes are read-only. Which HTTP status expresses this outcome?

opts.A: 403 Forbidden
opts.B: 401 Unauthorized
opts.C: 400 Bad Request
opts.D: 422 Unprocessable Content

exp: The server has successfully authenticated the caller and is refusing on authorization grounds, which is what 403 means. 401 is the frequent wrong pick: it signals that valid authentication credentials are absent or unusable, and re-presenting the same token would be the client's only recourse — pointless here, since the token is fine and the permission is not.

sub: Backend development in PHP and Python: REST APIs, CRUD, middleware, auth, sessions and ORM
q: A single-page app on https://app.example.com calls an API on https://api.example.com. The browser's preflight OPTIONS request returns 401, so no cross-origin call ever completes — yet the identical requests succeed from curl with the same valid token. What is the most likely cause?

opts.A: The API omits the Access-Control-Allow-Credentials header from its responses
opts.B: Browsers strip the Authorization header from preflight requests only when the target is served over HTTPS
opts.C: The authentication middleware is registered ahead of the CORS middleware, so it rejects the deliberately credential-less preflight before CORS can answer it
opts.D: OPTIONS is a non-idempotent method, so the API's rate-limiting middleware refuses to serve it

exp: A preflight OPTIONS request is generated by the browser and carries neither Authorization headers nor cookies by design, so any auth middleware sitting in front of the CORS middleware sees an unauthenticated request and answers 401 before the CORS headers are ever attached; registering CORS first, or exempting OPTIONS from auth, resolves it. A missing Access-Control-Allow-Credentials header would show up as a browser-blocked response on the real request, not as a 401 on the preflight.

sub: Backend development in PHP and Python: REST APIs, CRUD, middleware, auth, sessions and ORM
q: Doctrine ORM and Eloquent are both PHP persistence libraries, but they implement different data-access patterns. Which statement characterises the difference correctly?

opts.A: Eloquent is a Data Mapper whose plain models are persisted by a separate EntityManager, while Doctrine entities save themselves
opts.B: Eloquent is an Active Record implementation, where a model both maps a row and knows how to persist itself, while Doctrine is a Data Mapper that keeps entities free of persistence logic and delegates it to an EntityManager
opts.C: Both are Active Record implementations, differing only in whether mappings are declared as attributes or as properties on the model class
opts.D: Doctrine is an Active Record implementation tuned for read-heavy workloads, while Eloquent is a query builder that performs no object mapping

exp: Eloquent models inherit persistence behaviour — save(), delete() and the query interface live on the model itself, the defining trait of Active Record — whereas a Doctrine entity is an ordinary PHP object with no knowledge of the database, and the EntityManager performs the mapping. Option A is the same distinction stated with the two libraries swapped, which is the mistake worth catching.

sub: Backend development in PHP and Python: REST APIs, CRUD, middleware, auth, sessions and ORM
q:
In a Python service using the SQLAlchemy ORM:

user = session.get(User, 1)
user.email = "new@example.com"
session.commit()

No UPDATE statement appears anywhere in the code, yet the row changes. Which ORM mechanism accounts for this?

opts.A: The unit-of-work pattern — the Session tracks attribute changes on the instances it manages and flushes the resulting UPDATE as part of the commit
opts.B: session.get() returns a write-through proxy that pushes each attribute assignment to the database as the assignment happens
opts.C: The commit re-reads the object and rewrites every column of the row unconditionally, so no change tracking is needed
opts.D: The Session runs in autocommit mode by default, so each attribute assignment becomes its own transaction

exp: Objects loaded through a Session stay in its identity map, mutating a mapped attribute marks the instance dirty, and the flush that precedes commit emits an UPDATE covering the changed columns — that accumulate-then-flush behaviour is the unit-of-work pattern. Option B is the intuitive but wrong model: nothing whatsoever reaches the database at assignment time, which is why rolling back discards the edit.

sub: Backend development in PHP and Python: REST APIs, CRUD, middleware, auth, sessions and ORM
q: An API implements optimistic concurrency: clients GET a resource, receive an ETag, and echo it in an If-Match header on the follow-up PUT. Two clients edit the same resource, and the second PUT arrives carrying an ETag that no longer matches the stored representation. Which status should the server return?

opts.A: 409 Conflict
opts.B: 428 Precondition Required
opts.C: 423 Locked
opts.D: 412 Precondition Failed

exp: HTTP semantics say that when a conditional request header such as If-Match evaluates to false, the server must not perform the method and answers 412 Precondition Failed. 428 Precondition Required is the inverse situation — the server demanding a conditional header that the client failed to send — and here the client did send one.

sub: Backend development in PHP and Python: REST APIs, CRUD, middleware, auth, sessions and ORM
q: A PHP application stores credentials as password_hash($pw, PASSWORD_DEFAULT). A later PHP upgrade changes what PASSWORD_DEFAULT resolves to, and the team wants existing users silently migrated at their next successful login. Which built-in function performs exactly the check of whether a stored hash was produced with different parameters and therefore ought to be recomputed?

opts.A: password_get_info()
opts.B: password_needs_rehash()
opts.C: hash_equals()
opts.D: password_verify(), passing the desired algorithm as a third argument

exp: password_needs_rehash() compares the algorithm and options embedded in an existing hash against the ones supplied and returns true when they differ, so it is called right after a successful verify — the one moment the plaintext is available to rehash. password_get_info() merely reports what a hash was made with and makes no comparison and no decision, and password_verify() takes only the password and the hash.

sub: Git version control, Docker, CI/CD, Linux administration, Nginx and deployment
q: A developer adds the line `config/secrets.env` to the repository's root `.gitignore` and commits it, but `git status` continues to report modifications to `config/secrets.env`. What explains this, and what stops it?

opts.A: `.gitignore` entries must be anchored with a leading slash to match a path inside a subdirectory, so the entry should read `/config/secrets.env`
opts.B: A `.gitignore` in the repository root does not apply to subdirectories, so a separate `.gitignore` has to be placed inside `config/`
opts.C: `.gitignore` is consulted only for untracked paths, so a file already in the index stays tracked; `git rm --cached config/secrets.env` and a commit stop it being tracked
opts.D: An ignore rule takes effect only after `.gitignore` itself is pushed to the remote, so the entry does nothing until the branch is pushed

exp: Ignore rules are applied when Git decides whether to start tracking an untracked path; a path already recorded in the index is unaffected, so it must be removed from the index with `git rm --cached` while being left on disk. The leading-slash option is wrong because a slash only anchors the pattern to the repository root, which `config/secrets.env` already is — anchoring was never the problem.

sub: Git version control, Docker, CI/CD, Linux administration, Nginx and deployment
q: A feature branch has three commits that exist only locally. The developer runs `git reset --soft HEAD~2`. What is the state of the branch, index and working tree immediately afterwards?

opts.A: HEAD moves back two commits and the changes those commits introduced are discarded from both the index and the working tree
opts.B: HEAD moves back two commits, the changes those commits introduced are left staged in the index, and the working tree is untouched
opts.C: HEAD moves back two commits and the changes those commits introduced appear as unstaged modifications, with the index matching the new HEAD
opts.D: The branch pointer stays on the newest commit and only the index is rewound by two commits

exp: `--soft` moves the branch ref and HEAD only, leaving the index and working tree exactly as they were, which is why the squashed content shows up already staged and ready to be recommitted as one commit. The unstaged-modifications option describes `--mixed`, the default, which resets the index to the new HEAD but not the working tree; wholesale discarding is `--hard`.

sub: Git version control, Docker, CI/CD, Linux administration, Nginx and deployment
q:
A Node web application's Dockerfile contains, in this order:

    COPY . .
    RUN npm ci

Every build after a one-line source edit re-runs the full dependency install. Which change restores build-cache reuse for the install step?

opts.A: Move `RUN npm ci` above `COPY . .`, leaving both lines otherwise unchanged
opts.B: Add `--no-cache` to the `npm ci` invocation
opts.C: Replace `COPY . .` with `ADD . .`
opts.D: Copy `package.json` and `package-lock.json` alone, run `npm ci`, and only then `COPY . .`

exp: A layer's cache entry is invalidated when the contents it copies change, so copying the whole source tree before installing makes any source edit invalidate the install layer; copying just the manifest and lockfile first means the install layer is only rebuilt when dependencies actually change. Simply hoisting `RUN npm ci` above `COPY . .` fails outright, because at that point no `package.json` exists in the image for npm to read.

sub: Git version control, Docker, CI/CD, Linux administration, Nginx and deployment
q: A React application is packaged with a multi-stage Dockerfile whose final stage starts from `nginx:alpine` and copies only the built `dist/` directory out of the Node build stage. What is the principal advantage over a single-stage image that keeps the Node toolchain and serves the build itself?

opts.A: The shipped image contains no Node runtime, compilers or dev dependencies, which cuts both image size and the attack surface that has to be patched
opts.B: The intermediate build stage's layers are pushed alongside the final image and shared with other images, lowering total registry storage
opts.C: Nginx negotiates HTTP/3 for the static assets by default, which a Node-based static server cannot do
opts.D: The stages of a multi-stage build run in parallel, so the dependency install overlaps with the production bundle step

exp: The value of the pattern is that only the artefacts explicitly copied into the final stage survive into the shipped image, so build-time tooling and dev dependencies never become part of the deployed surface. The registry-storage option inverts the mechanism: intermediate stages are not part of the resulting image and are not pushed at all.

sub: Git version control, Docker, CI/CD, Linux administration, Nginx and deployment
q: In the install step of a CI job for a Node web application, why is `npm ci` normally preferred over `npm install`?

opts.A: `npm ci` installs only production dependencies, so devDependencies never reach the CI runner
opts.B: `npm ci` installs exactly the dependency tree recorded in `package-lock.json` and fails outright if the lockfile and `package.json` disagree, so the build is reproducible
opts.C: `npm ci` first refreshes `package-lock.json` to the newest versions permitted by the declared semver ranges, so CI always tests against current dependencies
opts.D: `npm ci` links packages from the runner's global cache instead of creating a local `node_modules` directory, so nothing has to be written to disk

exp: `npm ci` treats the lockfile as authoritative rather than as a hint, so it cannot silently resolve a different version than a developer got, and a lockfile that has drifted out of sync with `package.json` breaks the build instead of being quietly rewritten. The devDependencies option is wrong because omitting them is a separate choice controlled by `--omit=dev`; `npm ci` installs the full tree by default, which CI needs in order to run tests and linters.

sub: Git version control, Docker, CI/CD, Linux administration, Nginx and deployment
q: A web application's pipeline compiles the application from source once for the staging deployment and again for the production deployment, both from the same Git commit. Production deployments occasionally misbehave in ways the staging run that approved them did not. Which pipeline change most directly eliminates this class of failure?

opts.A: Pin the CI runner image to a fixed tag so that both builds begin from an identical base operating system
opts.B: Tag the Git commit before the production build so that both deployments are traceable to a single revision
opts.C: Build the artefact once and promote that same immutable artefact from staging into production, supplying environment-specific values as configuration at deploy time
opts.D: Re-run the full test suite against the production environment immediately after every deployment

exp: Two builds are two artefacts, and anything non-deterministic in the build — a floating transitive dependency, a differing toolchain, a stale cache — means the thing tested in staging is not the thing running in production; building once and promoting the identical artefact removes the divergence by construction. Pinning the runner image narrows one source of drift but still produces two separately built artefacts, so the failure mode survives.

sub: Git version control, Docker, CI/CD, Linux administration, Nginx and deployment
q: A Django application served by Gunicorn is managed as a systemd service on a Linux server. Which setting in its unit file causes systemd to bring the service back automatically when the process exits with a non-zero status?

opts.A: `Restart=on-failure` in the `[Service]` section
opts.B: `WantedBy=multi-user.target` in the `[Install]` section
opts.C: `After=network.target` in the `[Unit]` section
opts.D: `RemainAfterExit=yes` in the `[Service]` section

exp: `Restart=on-failure` is the directive that tells systemd to restart the unit when it terminates with a non-zero exit code or is killed by a signal. `RemainAfterExit=yes` is close in appearance but does the opposite of what is wanted: it makes systemd regard the unit as still active after its process has exited, so nothing is restarted; `WantedBy` only governs whether the unit starts at boot when enabled.

sub: Git version control, Docker, CI/CD, Linux administration, Nginx and deployment
q: Nginx terminates TLS at the edge and reverse-proxies to an application on 127.0.0.1:8000. The application's access log records every request as coming from 127.0.0.1. Assuming the application is already configured to trust a forwarded client-address header, which line added to the proxying `location` block gives it the real client address?

opts.A: `proxy_set_header Host $host;`
opts.B: `proxy_pass_request_headers on;`
opts.C: `real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For;`
opts.D: `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;`

exp: From the application's point of view the TCP peer genuinely is Nginx on the loopback address, so the client address has to be carried in a header that Nginx sets on the upstream request; `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` appends `$remote_addr` to any inbound `X-Forwarded-For` value. `real_ip_header` looks apt but solves the mirror-image problem — it tells *Nginx* to take its own `$remote_addr` from a header when Nginx itself sits behind another proxy, and it changes nothing about what the upstream receives.

sub: Git version control, Docker, CI/CD, Linux administration, Nginx and deployment
q: A client-side-routed single-page application is served by Nginx from `/var/www/app`, which contains `index.html` and a hashed asset bundle. Navigating within the app works, but reloading the browser on `/dashboard` returns 404. Which directive in the `location /` block fixes it?

opts.A: `autoindex on;`
opts.B: `try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;`
opts.C: `index index.html index.htm;`
opts.D: `rewrite ^/dashboard$ / permanent;`

exp: `/dashboard` exists only as a route inside the JavaScript router, not as a file on disk, so Nginx must fall back to serving `index.html` for any path it cannot resolve and let the client-side router read the URL; `try_files` with `/index.html` as its final fallback does exactly that while still serving real files such as the asset bundle directly. The `index` directive does not help because it only chooses a default file for requests that resolve to a directory, and `/dashboard` resolves to nothing at all.

sub: Web security: OWASP Top 10, SSL/TLS, CSRF, XSS and SQL injection prevention
q: An application's session cookie is set with SameSite=Lax. Which request originating from an attacker-controlled page will still arrive at the application carrying that cookie?

opts.A: An auto-submitting cross-site POST form targeting an application endpoint
opts.B: A cross-origin fetch() to the application issued with credentials: 'include'
opts.C: A top-level navigation to an application URL caused by the user clicking a link on the attacker's page
opts.D: An element on the attacker's page whose src points at an application URL

exp: SameSite=Lax withholds the cookie on all cross-site subresource and non-safe-method requests, but deliberately allows it on top-level navigations made with a safe method such as GET, so ordinary inbound links keep working. The auto-submitting POST form is the classic CSRF vector and is exactly what Lax blocks, which is why it is tempting but wrong.

sub: Web security: OWASP Top 10, SSL/TLS, CSRF, XSS and SQL injection prevention
q: A link-preview feature fetches any URL the user submits and returns the response body. An attacker submits a URL pointing at the cloud provider's link-local instance metadata endpoint and retrieves the instance's credentials. In the OWASP Top 10:2025, which category covers this class of flaw?

opts.A: A01:2025 - Broken Access Control
opts.B: A05:2025 - Injection
opts.C: A02:2025 - Security Misconfiguration
opts.D: A10:2025 - Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions

exp: Server-Side Request Forgery had its own category, A10:2021, in the previous edition, but the 2025 edition retired that standalone entry and folded CWE-918 into A01:2025 Broken Access Control, on the reasoning that making a server issue attacker-chosen requests to destinations it should not reach is an access-control failure between services. Injection is the nearest miss - the attacker does supply the input - but the flaw is not that the input gets parsed as code. Note the 2025 renumbering while revising: Injection moved to A05 and Security Misconfiguration to A02, so distractor numbering carried over from the 2021 list is itself a trap.
reviewFix: Re-keyed from the 2021 taxonomy to the 2025 one, and the keyed letter changed from D to A. The question pinned itself to '(2021 edition)' and so was internally consistent, but it drilled precisely the fact that has since been reversed: the OWASP Top 10:2025, published 6 November 2025, deleted SSRF as a standalone category and folded CWE-918 into A01:2025 Broken Access Control — verified on owasp.org/Top10/2025/A01_2025-Broken_Access_Control/, which names CWE-918 among its notable CWEs.
