sub: Web security: OWASP Top 10, SSL/TLS, CSRF, XSS and SQL injection prevention
q: An adversary passively records a site's encrypted TLS traffic today and obtains the server's long-term private key two years later. Which property, if the connections had it, keeps the recorded traffic undecryptable?

opts.A: Record protection with an AEAD cipher such as AES-GCM
opts.B: Forward secrecy from an ephemeral (EC)DHE key exchange, so session keys are never recoverable from the certificate's key
opts.C: Certificate pinning in the client
opts.D: Strict-Transport-Security sent with a long max-age

exp: Forward secrecy comes from deriving each session's keys through an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange whose private values are discarded, so the certificate key only authenticates the handshake and never encrypts the session keys - which is why TLS 1.3 dropped static RSA key transport entirely. AES-GCM protects each record's confidentiality and integrity in transit but says nothing about how the keys were established, so it does not help against a later key compromise.

sub: Web security: OWASP Top 10, SSL/TLS, CSRF, XSS and SQL injection prevention
q: Users reach a portal by typing the bare domain name, and an on-path attacker strips the HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect on that very first request. Which measure protects a user who has never visited the site before?

opts.A: Getting the domain added to the browsers' HSTS preload list
opts.B: Sending Strict-Transport-Security with a two-year max-age and includeSubDomains on every HTTPS response
opts.C: Marking every cookie Secure and HttpOnly
opts.D: Publishing a CAA DNS record naming the site's certificate authority

exp: An HSTS policy is trust-on-first-use: the browser only learns it after one successful HTTPS response, so the very first plaintext request remains strippable - the preload list closes that gap by shipping the policy inside the browser before any visit. Option B is correct practice and is in fact the prerequisite for preloading, but on its own it cannot protect a first-time visitor.

sub: Web security: OWASP Top 10, SSL/TLS, CSRF, XSS and SQL injection prevention
q: A report screen lets the user pick which column to sort by. The developer tries to bind that column name as a query placeholder, but the driver quotes it as a string literal and the ordering stops working. What is the correct way to make the feature both work and be injection-safe?

opts.A: Escape the value with the driver's string-escaping function before concatenating it into the ORDER BY clause
opts.B: Concatenate the value but reject any input containing a semicolon, a quote or the word UNION
opts.C: Compare the value against a fixed server-side allow-list of permitted column names and interpolate only the matching literal from that list
opts.D: Wrap the value in single quotes inside the ORDER BY clause so the database treats it as a string

exp: Placeholders bind values, not identifiers, so a table name, column name or sort direction can never be parameterised; the only safe substitute is to map user input onto a fixed set of identifiers the code already knows and emit one of those. Escaping (option A) is designed for string literals and does not make an identifier position safe, and denylisting keywords (option B) is defeated by inputs the list did not anticipate.

sub: Web security: OWASP Top 10, SSL/TLS, CSRF, XSS and SQL injection prevention
q: A page is served with the header Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self'. An attacker succeeds in reflecting the markup into that page. What happens when the image fails to load?

opts.A: The handler runs, because script-src governs <script> elements only and not event handler attributes
opts.B: The handler runs, because the injected markup is delivered from the page's own origin, which 'self' permits
opts.C: The handler is blocked only if the response additionally sends X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block
opts.D: The handler is blocked, because an inline event handler attribute counts as inline script and 'self' does not permit inline script

exp: CSP treats inline event handler attributes as inline script, so a script-src list that omits 'unsafe-inline' refuses to execute them. A nonce cannot rescue one: a nonce is carried on a <script> element, and an event handler attribute has nowhere to put it — attribute-style inline script is governed by script-src-attr, which only 'unsafe-inline', or 'unsafe-hashes' together with a matching hash, can permit. That is exactly why a nonce-based policy without 'unsafe-inline' blunts reflected XSS: the attacker cannot attach a nonce to injected markup. Option B confuses the origin that served the HTML with the origin of the script source: 'self' only whitelists externally loaded scripts from the same origin, never inline code.
reviewFix: Explanation fixed. The key and option text were correct, but the parenthetical '(and supplies no matching nonce or hash)' implied a nonce is a route to permitting an inline event handler attribute. It is not: nonces apply to elements, an onerror= attribute has no place to carry one, and attribute-style inline script is governed by script-src-attr, whose only permitting expressions are 'unsafe-inline' or 'unsafe-hashes' plus a matching hash. As written it would have led a reader to write a nonce policy believing it whitelisted handlers it silently does not. Key unchanged.

sub: Web security: OWASP Top 10, SSL/TLS, CSRF, XSS and SQL injection prevention
q: An application has an unfixed XSS flaw. Its session cookie is set Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict. What is the accurate assessment of the attacker's position?

opts.A: The injected script cannot read the cookie value, but it runs inside the application's own origin and can still drive authenticated state-changing requests to which the browser attaches the cookie
opts.B: SameSite=Strict causes the browser to refuse the injected script's requests to the application, because they originate from attacker-supplied markup
opts.C: HttpOnly prevents the injected script from executing in the first place
opts.D: Secure means the cookie is stored encrypted in the browser's cookie jar, so it cannot be exfiltrated even by script

exp: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie, but the injected script executes with the page's origin and privileges, so it can perform the actions the session authorises without ever seeing the token - which is why cookie flags mitigate but never substitute for fixing XSS. Option B misreads SameSite: it is evaluated against the site of the request's initiating document, and here that document is the application itself, so the requests are same-site.

sub: Web security: OWASP Top 10, SSL/TLS, CSRF, XSS and SQL injection prevention
q: A newly deployed HTTPS site loads without warnings in every desktop browser, but a curl call from a server fails with 'SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate'. What is the most likely cause?

opts.A: The leaf certificate has expired, and browsers ignore expiry for certificates from well-known CAs
opts.B: The server presents the leaf certificate but omits the intermediate CA certificate; browsers complete the chain from cached intermediates or by fetching the issuer, while curl's trust store holds only roots
opts.C: The certificate's subject alternative names do not include the hostname being requested
opts.D: curl does not send SNI, so the server answers with the default virtual host's certificate

exp: That specific error means chain building stopped short of a trusted root, and the usual cause is a server bundle missing the intermediate - browsers paper over it because they cache intermediates seen elsewhere and can fetch the issuer named in the certificate, which command-line clients generally do not do. A hostname mismatch (option C) would produce a distinct 'subject name does not match' error and would fail in the browser too.

sub: Web security: OWASP Top 10, SSL/TLS, CSRF, XSS and SQL injection prevention
q: A stateless JSON API cannot keep a per-session CSRF token server-side, so it instead requires every state-changing request to carry a custom header such as X-CSRF-Token. Why does merely requiring that header defeat classic CSRF?

opts.A: Because an attacker's page has no way to discover which header name the application expects
opts.B: Because browsers refuse to attach cookies to any request that carries a custom header
opts.C: Because a custom header makes the request non-simple, so the browser must first send a CORS preflight, and without a permissive CORS response the state-changing request is never delivered
opts.D: Because HTML forms cannot set request headers, and forms are the only cross-site request vector available to an attacker

exp: Only a short safelist of headers may appear on a cross-origin request without a preflight; adding any other header forces an OPTIONS preflight that the application simply declines, so the real request never reaches the endpoint. Option D gets the form half right but is wrong overall - script-driven fetch and XHR are also cross-site vectors, and it is CORS, not the absence of those vectors, that stops them.

sub: Architecture and scale: MVC, microservices, SOLID, event-driven systems, caching and queues
q: A `Rectangle` class exposes `setWidth()` and `setHeight()`. A `Square` subclass overrides both so that setting one dimension silently sets the other. Reporting code that has always worked against a `Rectangle` reference — set width 5, set height 4, expect area 20 — starts producing 16 once a `Square` instance is passed in. Which SOLID principle has been violated?

opts.A: Single Responsibility Principle
opts.B: Interface Segregation Principle
opts.C: Liskov Substitution Principle
opts.D: Open/Closed Principle

exp: Liskov substitution requires that an instance of a subtype can replace the supertype without breaking any guarantee the caller was entitled to rely on, and `Square` breaks the independent-dimensions contract that `Rectangle` advertises. The Open/Closed Principle is the tempting alternative but it concerns whether new behaviour can be added without editing existing code, and nothing here was extended by modification — the inheritance itself is what is unsound.

sub: Architecture and scale: MVC, microservices, SOLID, event-driven systems, caching and queues
q: A team argues that because every collaborator is supplied through a dependency-injection container rather than constructed with `new`, the codebase satisfies the Dependency Inversion Principle. What does DIP additionally require that a DI container by itself does not give you?

opts.A: That object graphs be wired by a framework rather than by hand-written factory code
opts.B: That the high-level policy and the low-level implementation both depend on an abstraction defined in terms of the high-level module's needs, rather than the policy depending on the concrete implementation
opts.C: That every concrete class in the system be paired with an interface, even where only one implementation exists
opts.D: That dependencies be resolved at runtime from configuration rather than being fixed at compile time

exp: DIP is a statement about the direction of source-level dependencies — the policy layer owns the abstraction and the detail layer conforms to it — so a container that injects a concrete database class into a service still inverts nothing. Runtime resolution from configuration is a real capability of DI containers and sounds authoritative, but late binding is a mechanism, not the ownership rule DIP is about.

sub: Architecture and scale: MVC, microservices, SOLID, event-driven systems, caching and queues
q: An order-placement flow spans an Order service, a Payment service and an Inventory service, each owning its own database. The architect rules out holding one ACID transaction open across all three. Which approach keeps the business outcome consistent instead?

opts.A: Two-phase commit driven by a coordinator in the API gateway
opts.B: Optimistic locking with a version column on the order row, retried on conflict
opts.C: Giving the three services a shared schema so a single database transaction can span them
opts.D: A saga: a sequence of local transactions in which each service commits its own step and publishes an event, with compensating transactions undoing earlier steps if a later one fails

exp: A saga trades atomicity for eventual consistency, replacing rollback with explicit compensating actions such as refunding a payment or releasing a stock reservation, which is exactly the pattern for cross-service consistency without a distributed lock. Two-phase commit is the most tempting option because it does deliver atomicity, but it is precisely the distributed transaction that was ruled out — the coordinator becomes a blocking single point of failure holding locks across all three databases.

sub: Architecture and scale: MVC, microservices, SOLID, event-driven systems, caching and queues
q: A recommendation service begins responding in about 30 seconds instead of 50 milliseconds. The checkout service, which calls it synchronously on the product page, exhausts its request-handling thread pool waiting, and within minutes checkout stops serving even requests that never touch recommendations. Which pattern is specifically intended to stop this propagation?

opts.A: A circuit breaker that opens after a failure or latency threshold and fails fast on the recommendation call until the dependency is probed healthy again
opts.B: Retrying each recommendation call with exponential backoff and jitter
opts.C: Horizontally scaling the checkout service to more replicas
opts.D: Raising the HTTP client timeout on the recommendation call so slow responses still succeed

exp: The failure is resource exhaustion caused by threads parked on a slow dependency, so the fix is to stop calling it: an open circuit breaker returns immediately with a fallback, freeing capacity for unrelated work, and a bulkhead limiting that dependency to its own bounded pool serves the same containment goal. Retry with backoff is a genuinely good practice for transient errors, which makes it tempting, but against an overloaded dependency it multiplies in-flight calls and accelerates the collapse; raising the timeout holds threads even longer.

sub: Architecture and scale: MVC, microservices, SOLID, event-driven systems, caching and queues
q: A service publishes `AccountDebited` and `AccountCredited` events to an Apache Kafka topic with six partitions, consumed by a consumer group. Events concerning the same account must be processed in the order they were produced, while events for different accounts may be processed in parallel. Which measure achieves this?

opts.A: Configuring the consumer group with exactly as many consumer instances as there are partitions
opts.B: Producing every event with the account identifier as the message key, so that all events for one account are routed to the same partition
opts.C: Setting `auto.offset.reset` to `earliest` on the consumer group
opts.D: Increasing the topic's partition count so each account is statistically likely to get its own partition

exp: Kafka guarantees ordering only within a single partition, and the default partitioner hashes the message key, so keying by account identifier pins one account's whole event stream to one partition read by one consumer in the group. Adding partitions is the opposite of a fix — it spreads an unkeyed account's events across more partitions and destroys any ordering, and no partition count makes the routing deterministic without a key.

sub: Architecture and scale: MVC, microservices, SOLID, event-driven systems, caching and queues
q: A worker consuming an Amazon SQS standard queue throws an unhandled exception on one malformed message. The message's visibility timeout expires, it returns to the queue, the worker picks it up and crashes again, and this repeats indefinitely while healthy messages pile up behind it. Which queue configuration is the standard remedy for this poison-message loop?

opts.A: Lengthening the visibility timeout so the message stays invisible longer between attempts
opts.B: Converting the queue to FIFO so the message is delivered exactly once
opts.C: A redrive policy that moves the message to a dead-letter queue once its receive count exceeds `maxReceiveCount`
opts.D: Adding more worker instances so the malformed message occupies a smaller share of consumer capacity

exp: A redrive policy counts deliveries per message and diverts anything exceeding `maxReceiveCount` to a dead-letter queue, quarantining the bad message for offline inspection while the main queue drains. FIFO queues are the most plausible distractor because they do offer exactly-once processing within the deduplication window, but that governs duplicate sends, not repeated redelivery after a consumer failure — a FIFO queue would in fact make things worse by blocking the whole message group behind the poison message.

sub: Architecture and scale: MVC, microservices, SOLID, event-driven systems, caching and queues
q: A write-heavy service places a cache in front of its database. The design requires the lowest achievable write latency and explicitly accepts that a crash of a cache node may lose the most recent writes that have not yet been flushed to the database. Which cache write strategy is being described?

opts.A: Write-behind (write-back), where the write is acknowledged from the cache and persisted to the database asynchronously in batches
opts.B: Write-through, where every write goes to the cache and the database as one synchronous operation
opts.C: Cache-aside, where the application writes to the database and invalidates the cached entry
opts.D: Refresh-ahead, where the cache proactively reloads entries that are about to expire

exp: Write-behind acknowledges the client as soon as the cache accepts the write and drains to the database later, which is what buys the low latency and what creates the durability window the requirement concedes. Write-through is the natural competitor and shares the same access shape, but because it commits to the database before acknowledging it has strictly higher write latency and loses nothing on a cache failure.

sub: Architecture and scale: MVC, microservices, SOLID, event-driven systems, caching and queues
q: A frontend codebase is described as MVVM rather than MVC. Which statement identifies the defining structural difference?

opts.A: MVVM eliminates the model layer, so the view obtains data by calling the backend API directly
opts.B: In MVVM the view model produces the rendered markup while the view holds the application state
opts.C: MVVM applies only to server-rendered pages, whereas MVC applies only to client-side applications
opts.D: In MVVM the view binds declaratively to observable state exposed by a view model that holds no reference to the view, so state changes propagate through the binding rather than through a controller that handles each interaction

exp: MVVM's distinguishing mechanism is data binding: the view model publishes observable state and commands and is deliberately ignorant of any view, which is what makes it unit-testable without a rendering surface. The claim that MVVM drops the model is the most seductive wrong answer because view models are often mistaken for models, but MVVM keeps a domain/model layer and adds the view model as a presentation-shaped adapter over it.

q: A Node.js project's `package.json` declares a dependency as `"lodash": "^4.17.20"` and the lockfile has been deleted. Under npm's semantic-versioning range rules, which of these versions may `npm install` resolve the dependency to?
exp: The caret range `^4.17.20` admits any version at or above 4.17.20 but below the next major, i.e. `>=4.17.20 <5.0.0`, so 4.18.1 is in range and npm will take the highest published match. 4.17.19 is the trap: it looks close enough to satisfy the caret, but it is lower than the stated minimum, and 5.0.1 crosses the major boundary the caret exists to hold.

sub: AI-assisted web development, generative AI APIs, Model Context Protocol, analytics, ethics and law
q: An MCP server for a deployment platform has to expose two capabilities: the text of a service's log file, which the host application should be able to fetch and place into the model's context on demand, and an operation that restarts that service. Which MCP primitives fit these two respectively?

opts.A: Both as tools, since either way the host has to make a call to the server
opts.B: The log file as a resource and the restart as a tool
opts.C: The log file as a prompt and the restart as a resource
opts.D: Both as resources, with the restart modelled as a writable resource

exp: MCP resources are addressable, readable context that a client retrieves and hands to the model, whereas tools are invocable functions with side effects that the model can choose to call — a log file is context, a restart is an action. Option A is tempting because both involve a round trip to the server, but it discards precisely the distinction MCP draws so that a host can apply different trust and approval rules to reading data versus performing actions; prompts, the third primitive, are reusable templated interactions, not file contents.

q: Messages exchanged between a host application's MCP client and an MCP server are encoded using which pre-existing specification?

opts.A: JSON-RPC 2.0
opts.B: gRPC with Protocol Buffers
opts.C: GraphQL queries over HTTP POST
opts.D: SOAP 1.2 envelopes over HTTP

exp: MCP defines its requests, responses and notifications as JSON-RPC 2.0 messages, which is what lets the identical message shapes travel over a local stdio pipe or an HTTP-based transport without change. gRPC is the natural guess because it is the usual choice for machine-to-machine RPC, but it requires a binary codec and HTTP/2 and so would not suit the plain stdio local-subprocess server that MCP is built to support.

q: Reviewing code produced by an AI coding assistant, a developer finds an import of an npm package whose name resembles, but is not, a well-known library. npm install succeeds and CI is green. Why is this a supply-chain concern rather than merely a typo?

opts.A: The invented name will break semantic-version resolution the next time the lockfile is refreshed
opts.B: npm silently substitutes the nearest published package name, so runtime behaviour differs from the source
opts.C: No type declarations will be found, so TypeScript degrades the import to any and hides errors
opts.D: Models invent the same plausible package names repeatedly, and attackers pre-register those names, so a successful install pulls attacker-controlled code

exp: Hallucinated dependency names cluster rather than being random, so an attacker who publishes them obtains code execution in every build and developer machine that installs one — which is why the install succeeding is the alarming outcome, not a failing one. npm performs no nearest-name substitution: an unpublished name simply 404s, so the fact that it resolved at all is the evidence that somebody registered it.

sub: AI-assisted web development, generative AI APIs, Model Context Protocol, analytics, ethics and law
q: A support chat widget calls a stateless hosted generative AI chat-completion API, so the backend resends the whole transcript on every turn. Ignoring prompt caching, and assuming the transcript still fits inside the context window, how do the cumulative billed input tokens for one session grow with the number of turns n?

opts.A: Roughly linearly in n, because exactly one request is issued per turn
opts.B: Roughly with n squared, because each turn resends everything that preceded it
opts.C: Constant after the first turn, because the provider deduplicates context it has already seen in the session
opts.D: Bounded by the model's context window, so the session's cost stops rising once that size is reached

exp: Turn k carries about k turns' worth of transcript, and summing k from 1 to n produces an n-squared term, so a long conversation costs far more than n times the opening request. Option D confuses a per-request limit with a per-session total: the context window caps how much any single call may carry, but every later call still bills that retained context again.

sub: AI-assisted web development, generative AI APIs, Model Context Protocol, analytics, ethics and law
q: A first-party web analytics script must post a small end-of-session payload as the user navigates away, but requests started from a visibilitychange or unload handler are frequently cancelled when the document is torn down. Which browser API was introduced specifically to hand such a request to the user agent for delivery after the page is gone?

opts.A: navigator.sendBeacon()
opts.B: window.requestIdleCallback()
opts.C: A synchronous XMLHttpRequest issued inside the unload handler
opts.D: A beforeunload listener that returns a string

exp: sendBeacon() queues a small POST with the user agent, which undertakes to send it even after the document unloads, and it returns immediately so navigation is never delayed. Synchronous XHR in unload was the old workaround that sendBeacon exists to replace — browsers now block or ignore it precisely because it stalls the next navigation.

sub: AI-assisted web development, generative AI APIs, Model Context Protocol, analytics, ethics and law
q: A Kubernetes Deployment proxies user requests to an external generative AI provider; each request occupies a pod for 20-40 seconds while awaiting the upstream. Under load, queueing latency climbs steeply, but the HorizontalPodAutoscaler targeting 70% CPU utilisation reports the pods at about 5% CPU and never scales out. What explains this, and what is the correct fix?

opts.A: The CPU target is set too high; lowering it to 30% will make the same signal trigger scale-out
opts.B: The pods declare no CPU requests, so the HPA cannot compute utilisation; adding requests restores scaling
opts.C: The pods are blocked on I/O so CPU stays low; autoscale instead on a metric reflecting concurrency, such as in-flight requests or queue depth
opts.D: The readiness probe marks pods unready during long requests, so the HPA excludes them when averaging the metric

exp: The workload is I/O-bound on the upstream API, so CPU is a poor proxy for saturation — the resource actually exhausted is concurrent in-flight requests per pod, which is what the autoscaler must observe via a custom or external metric. Lowering the target, as option A proposes, changes nothing when measured utilisation is 5%: the threshold is not the problem, the choice of signal is; and the reported 5% figure shows utilisation is being computed, so option B's missing-requests scenario is not what is happening.

sub: AI-assisted web development, generative AI APIs, Model Context Protocol, analytics, ethics and law
q: A state government department discovers that its public web portal has been defaced and a table of registered users exfiltrated. Under the CERT-In directions issued in April 2022, within what period of noticing such an incident must it be reported to CERT-In?

opts.A: 72 hours
opts.B: 24 hours
opts.C: 30 days
opts.D: 6 hours

exp: The 2022 directions require the specified categories of cyber incident to be reported to CERT-In within six hours of noticing them or being brought to notice, a far tighter window than practitioners expect. Option A is the trap because 72 hours is the GDPR breach-notification deadline, which is frequently and wrongly assumed to apply in India; the same CERT-In directions also require ICT system logs to be maintained for 180 days within Indian jurisdiction.

sub: AI-assisted web development, generative AI APIs, Model Context Protocol, analytics, ethics and law
q: A web assistant fetches third-party pages and summarises them, and is also connected to an MCP server that can send email on the user's behalf. One retrieved page contains text instructing the assistant to forward the user's recent messages to an outside address. Which mitigation actually addresses this class of attack?

opts.A: Adding a line to the system prompt telling the model to disregard any instructions found inside retrieved content
opts.B: Enforcing authorisation and explicit user confirmation at the tool layer, so a send action cannot occur on the model's decision alone
opts.C: HTML-escaping the retrieved page before inserting its text into the prompt
opts.D: Lowering the sampling temperature so the model's output becomes more deterministic

exp: Untrusted retrieved text and trusted instructions reach the model as one undifferentiated token stream, so no wording inside the prompt reliably separates them; the durable control sits outside the model, in least-privilege tool scopes and a confirmation step before any side-effecting call. Option A is the usual first attempt and is defeated by rephrased injections, because it asks the model to police the very boundary it cannot perceive; escaping HTML does nothing, since the payload is ordinary prose, not markup.

sub: Distributed, edge and cloud computing; NIST cloud architecture
q: A cloud provider's console shows a customer, in near real time, the GB-hours of storage and vCPU-seconds each project has consumed, and bills strictly on those counters. Which of the five essential characteristics in the NIST definition of cloud computing does this most directly illustrate?

opts.A: Rapid elasticity
opts.B: Measured service
opts.C: Resource pooling
opts.D: On-demand self-service

exp: Measured service is NIST's term for metering resource use at a level of abstraction appropriate to the service, with usage monitored, controlled and reported transparently to both provider and consumer. Rapid elasticity is about capacity following demand, not about the meter that records it.

sub: Distributed, edge and cloud computing; NIST cloud architecture
q: A firm sits between a government department and three cloud providers: it combines their services into one composite offering, adds single sign-on and a consolidated bill, and negotiates terms on the department's behalf. In the NIST cloud computing reference architecture, which actor is this firm?

opts.A: Cloud auditor
opts.B: Cloud carrier
opts.C: Cloud broker
opts.D: Cloud provider

exp: The cloud broker manages the use, performance and delivery of cloud services and negotiates relationships between providers and consumers, with service intermediation, aggregation and arbitrage as its named functions. The cloud auditor only conducts independent assessment of services, operations, performance and security, and never resells or aggregates them.

sub: Distributed, edge and cloud computing; NIST cloud architecture
q: A globally replicated profile store keeps accepting reads and writes on both sides of a network partition and merges the diverged versions after the partition heals. Users occasionally read a value older than one they just wrote. In CAP terms, what does this describe?

opts.A: Availability and partition tolerance are chosen, so a read is not guaranteed to reflect the most recent acknowledged write
opts.B: Consistency and partition tolerance are chosen, so the stale reads must be a client-side caching defect rather than a consequence of the design
opts.C: Consistency and availability are chosen, and because the replicas sit inside one provider's network a partition cannot arise
opts.D: All three properties are achieved, because eventual consistency is strong consistency with a bounded delay

exp: A partition forces a choice, and staying writable on both sides is the AP choice: until the replicas converge, a read may legitimately miss the newest acknowledged write. Option D is the standard misreading — eventual consistency promises convergence eventually, with no bound and no guarantee that any particular read is current.

sub: Distributed, edge and cloud computing; NIST cloud architecture
q: A plant streams video from 200 cameras to a cloud region for defect detection. Alerts are needed within 30 seconds, a deadline the existing cloud round trip already meets comfortably. The team moves the detection model onto an on-site edge server that uploads only short clips of detected defects. What does this change primarily achieve?

opts.A: It removes the plant's need for wide-area connectivity, since all processing is now local
opts.B: It eliminates round-trip latency that would otherwise cause the 30-second deadline to be missed
opts.C: It makes each camera's detection results strongly consistent with the central database
opts.D: It cuts the sustained upstream bandwidth the site must carry, because only event clips rather than continuous streams cross the wide-area link

exp: Filtering at the edge changes what crosses the wide-area link from 200 continuous streams to occasional clips, which is a bandwidth and transport-cost reduction rather than a latency one. Option B is ruled out by the stem, which states the cloud round trip already meets the 30-second deadline; option A is wrong because the site still uploads clips and must be managed remotely.

sub: Distributed, edge and cloud computing; NIST cloud architecture
q: A replicated key-value store keeps N = 5 replicas. A write is acknowledged once W = 3 replicas confirm it, and a read consults R = 2 replicas. Under the usual quorum rule, is every read guaranteed to observe the most recently acknowledged write?

opts.A: Yes — W = 3 is a majority of the replicas, and a majority write by itself guarantees any later read observes it
opts.B: No — R + W is not greater than N, so a read set can consist entirely of the two replicas that did not take the write
opts.C: Yes — the overlap condition is R + W ≥ N, and 2 + 3 satisfies it
opts.D: No — read sets and write sets can overlap only when R = N, so any smaller R makes stale reads certain

exp: Quorum overlap requires R + W > N; here 2 + 3 = 5 exactly equals N, so the two replicas a reader consults can be precisely the two that missed the write. Option C is the off-by-one that makes this configuration look safe, stating the condition as ≥ instead of >.

sub: Distributed, edge and cloud computing; NIST cloud architecture
q: Four state departments jointly commission a cloud environment that only those four may use, sharing it because they are bound by the same data-handling and compliance rules. A private vendor owns and operates it, hosted in the vendor's own data centre. Under NIST SP 800-145, which deployment model is this?

opts.A: Community cloud, because it is provisioned for exclusive use by a specific community of consumers from organisations that have shared concerns, and it may be owned and operated by a third party off premises
opts.B: Public cloud, because a commercial vendor owns the infrastructure and hosts it in its own data centre
opts.C: Private cloud, because access is restricted to a named set of government departments rather than open to the general public
opts.D: Hybrid cloud, because several distinct organisations are bound together into a single environment

exp: NIST defines a community cloud as infrastructure provisioned for exclusive use by a specific community of consumers from organisations that have shared concerns — it gives mission, security requirements, policy and compliance considerations as the examples — and expressly allows it to be owned, managed and operated by a third party and to exist off premises. Private cloud is the near miss: it is equally non-public, but it is provisioned for a single organisation comprising multiple consumers, whereas here four separate departments share one environment on the strength of a common concern. Hybrid cloud means a composition of two or more distinct cloud infrastructures bound together, not several tenants of one.
reviewFix: Rewritten from private cloud to community cloud. Both blind passes independently found this a duplicate of GEN-T2U4-014: the same load-bearing NIST sentence, the same trap that vendor-owned and off-premises implies public cloud, and near-verbatim the same correct-option wording — one revision card printed twice, which they slipped past because the two sit under different sub-topic tags. Both judged 014 the stronger of the pair, since it makes the candidate apply the rule to a scenario rather than recall a definition, so 014 is kept unchanged and 006 is re-pointed at the community cloud model, which nothing else in either unit tested. The new stem, options and explanation are written against the deployment-model definitions extracted verbatim from the published NIST SP 800-145 PDF, not from recall.

sub: Distributed, edge and cloud computing; NIST cloud architecture
q: A service invokes a peer over the network and the call times out. Compared with a function call failing inside a single process, what is the fundamental new difficulty this introduces?

opts.A: The caller cannot tell whether the peer never received the request, is merely slow, or executed it and lost the reply, so the outcome of the operation is unknown
opts.B: The failure is handled entirely by the transport layer, so the application code needs no new logic
opts.C: The peer's failure necessarily leaves the whole system unavailable, unlike a local exception which is contained
opts.D: A timeout in a distributed system always means the peer crashed, so the caller can safely assume the request did not run

exp: A timeout carries no information about whether the remote side executed the request, which is why distributed designs need idempotency keys, retries and reconciliation rather than plain exception handling. Option D states the opposite and is the assumption that produces duplicate side effects: a timed-out request may well have committed on the peer.

sub: Distributed, edge and cloud computing; NIST cloud architecture
q: A datacentre team calls its on-premises cluster 'scalable' because more nodes can be racked once a capacity request is approved. Judged against NIST's essential characteristic of rapid elasticity, what is still missing?

opts.A: Provisioning must be fully automatic, since the definition requires automation in every case
opts.B: The provider must actually hold unlimited physical capacity behind the service
opts.C: Capacity must be added by moving to larger machines rather than by adding more of them
opts.D: Capacity must be both acquired and released rapidly and in proportion to current demand, without waiting on a procurement or approval cycle

exp: NIST's rapid elasticity requires capabilities to be provisioned and released so as to scale rapidly outward and inward commensurate with demand — release matters as much as acquisition, and an approval cycle defeats 'rapid'. Option A overreads the definition, which says elasticity is automatic only in some cases, and option B overreads it in the other direction: capacity need only appear unlimited to the consumer.

sub: Deployment and service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
q: A department runs an internal private cloud and separately subscribes to a public-cloud SaaS email service. The two share no data, no tooling and no identity integration. Which requirement of the NIST SP 800-145 hybrid cloud definition does this arrangement fail to meet?

opts.A: Both constituent infrastructures must be operated by the same cloud provider
opts.B: The same workload must be running simultaneously on the private and the public infrastructure
opts.C: The constituent infrastructures must remain distinct entities yet be bound together by standardised or proprietary technology that enables data and application portability
opts.D: At least one of the constituent infrastructures must be a community cloud

exp: NIST defines hybrid cloud as a composition of two or more distinct cloud infrastructures that remain unique entities but are bound together by technology enabling data and application portability, so merely holding two unrelated subscriptions is not a composition. B is the tempting one because cloud bursting is NIST's own illustration of such binding, but bursting is one permitted use of the binding, not a requirement that both infrastructures run the workload at once.

sub: Deployment and service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
q: Under the NIST SP 800-145 definition of Infrastructure as a Service, which of the following is the consumer said to control?

opts.A: The hypervisor's scheduling and memory-overcommit policy on the physical host
opts.B: Operating systems, storage and deployed applications, together with limited control of select networking components such as host firewalls
opts.C: The provider's underlying storage fabric and physical network topology
opts.D: The physical rack and data-hall placement of the servers running its instances

exp: The IaaS definition states that the consumer does not manage or control the underlying cloud infrastructure but has control over operating systems, storage and deployed applications, and possibly limited control of select networking components such as host firewalls. A is the near-miss: IaaS hands the consumer virtual machines, but the hypervisor that schedules them stays on the provider's side of the line.

sub: Deployment and service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
q: A critical vulnerability is disclosed in the guest operating system's TLS library. The same application is deployed three ways: (i) on an IaaS virtual machine the team launched from its own image, (ii) on a PaaS platform to which the team uploads only a deployable artefact, and (iii) as a function on a serverless FaaS platform. In which deployments must the customer itself apply the operating-system patch?

opts.A: (i) only
opts.B: (i) and (ii) only
opts.C: (ii) and (iii) only
opts.D: (i) and (iii) only

exp: Patching the guest operating system falls to the customer only where the customer supplies and boots the OS image, which is exactly the boundary that defines IaaS; PaaS and FaaS platforms both supply and maintain the operating system underneath the customer's code. B tempts because a PaaS consumer still owns and uploads the artefact, but that artefact is the application, not the operating system.

sub: Deployment and service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
q: Which characteristic most fundamentally distinguishes a Function-as-a-Service deployment from a PaaS deployment of the same application?

opts.A: In the default pay-per-use model, capacity is allocated per invocation and no compute is charged while no requests are being served, so there is no baseline instance count to provision
opts.B: Only PaaS lets the consumer choose the programming language and runtime version
opts.C: Only FaaS provides automatic scaling; PaaS deployments must be resized by hand
opts.D: Only PaaS runs on virtualised infrastructure, whereas FaaS executes directly on bare metal

exp: FaaS removes the provisioned instance from the default model: the platform creates execution capacity per event, scales to zero when idle, and bills on invocations and execution time rather than on running instances. The exception worth holding is that every major platform now sells an opt-in always-warm tier — AWS Lambda Provisioned Concurrency, Azure Functions always-ready instances, Cloud Run and Cloud Functions min-instances — which does keep initialised instances and does bill for them while idle, trading the scale-to-zero saving for the elimination of cold starts. C is the popular near-miss, since mainstream PaaS offerings have shipped autoscaling for years, so automatic scaling by itself does not separate the two models.
reviewFix: Option A and the explanation qualified to the default consumption model. Both blind passes flagged that 'nothing is charged while no requests are being served, so there is no provisioned instance count at all' has not been universally true of FaaS since 2019: AWS Lambda Provisioned Concurrency bills for the configured concurrency whether or not it serves a request, and Azure Functions always-ready instances and GCP min-instances behave the same way — on all three major platforms a FaaS deployment can have exactly a provisioned instance count and an idle charge. The distinction being tested is real and the key is still the only defensible option, but it is now scoped to the default model and the always-warm tiers are named as the exception. Key A unchanged.

sub: Deployment and service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
q: A file-upload feature writes user files to a local directory and later serves them back from there. It works on an IaaS virtual machine. Redeployed unchanged onto a PaaS platform running several application instances behind the platform's router, some uploads return 404 on a later request and all of them vanish after a redeploy. What explains this?

opts.A: The platform mounts the application's filesystem read-only, so the writes are silently discarded
opts.B: The platform's router strips multipart request bodies unless the application declares a file-upload route
opts.C: The platform packages the application immutably at build time, so any runtime write takes effect only after a fresh deployment
opts.D: Each instance has its own ephemeral local filesystem and requests are spread across instances, so a file written on one instance is neither visible to the others nor durable across redeploys

exp: The PaaS model treats application instances as disposable and interchangeable, so local disk is scratch space tied to one instance's lifetime, which is why uploads belong in an object store or an attached managed volume. A is the tempting alternative, but the writes plainly succeed - the file is readable immediately afterwards from the instance that stored it, which a read-only mount would not allow.

sub: Deployment and service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
q: A state department contracts a vendor to build, own and operate a cloud environment that only that department may use, hosted entirely in the vendor's own data centre. Under NIST SP 800-145, which deployment model is this?

opts.A: Private cloud, because the model is defined by provisioning for exclusive use by a single organisation, and the infrastructure may be owned, managed and operated by a third party and sit off premises
opts.B: Public cloud, because the infrastructure is owned by a commercial provider and located outside the department's premises
opts.C: Hybrid cloud, because operational responsibility is split between the department and the vendor
opts.D: Community cloud, because a government body and a commercial vendor both participate in it

exp: NIST defines private cloud by exclusivity of use rather than by ownership or location, and explicitly permits the infrastructure to be owned, managed and operated by a third party and to exist off premises. B is the standard trap: vendor-owned and off-premises does describe most public clouds, but public cloud is defined by provisioning for open use by the general public, which this environment is not.

sub: Deployment and service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
q: A function on a serverless FaaS platform reads messages from a queue and opens a connection to a managed relational database at the start of each invocation. During a traffic spike the platform runs roughly 800 concurrent executions and the function starts failing. What is the most likely cause?

opts.A: The queue stops delivering messages, because a FaaS function can consume a queue only one message at a time
opts.B: The database refuses new connections once its configured maximum is reached, because each concurrent execution environment holds a connection of its own
opts.C: Cold starts serialise the invocations, so the queue's visibility timeout expires before any handler can finish
opts.D: The platform transparently pools connections across execution environments, so the surplus connections are queued until they time out

exp: FaaS scales out by creating many independent execution environments, so consumer concurrency translates almost one-to-one into database connections and quickly exhausts a relational database's connection limit; the usual remedy is a connection pooler or proxy between the function and the database. D is tempting but backwards - no mainstream FaaS platform pools application-level database connections on the consumer's behalf.

sub: Deployment and service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
q: A customer of a multi-tenant SaaS application asks the vendor to keep its tenant on the previous release for six months while it revalidates internal processes. The vendor replies that this is not possible. Which property of the SaaS model explains that answer?

opts.A: Under SaaS it is the consumer, not the provider, who is responsible for applying application updates
opts.B: SaaS is defined by a dedicated application instance per tenant, and the vendor will not fund a second instance
opts.C: All tenants are served by one running version of the provider's application with tenant data separated logically, so there is no per-tenant build to hold back
opts.D: The provider's SLA obliges it to run only the most recent release in order to meet its availability commitment

exp: In SaaS the consumer uses the provider's application running on the provider's infrastructure and controls only limited user-specific configuration settings; a single shared codebase serving every tenant is what makes that model work, and it leaves no per-tenant version to freeze. B inverts the model, since a dedicated instance per tenant describes single-tenant hosting, which is precisely what multi-tenancy is not.

sub: Deployment and service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless

opts.A: Concurrent invocations share a single event loop, so pending promises are cancelled whenever any handler returns
opts.B: Returning a 2xx status causes the platform to discard everything the invocation did after the response was built
opts.C: FaaS runtimes forbid outbound network calls from a handler unless the call is awaited
opts.D: Once the handler returns, the platform may freeze or reclaim the execution environment, so work that was not awaited is not guaranteed to run to completion

exp: A FaaS platform treats the handler's return as the end of the invocation and may freeze the execution environment immediately, leaving the un-awaited promise suspended - sometimes finished much later by a subsequent invocation that reuses the same environment, which is why the records appear intermittently rather than never. B describes a similar outcome but blames the status code; the freeze happens on return whatever the handler returned.

sub: Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
q: A data centre reports a Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of 1.5. The operations team then consolidates workloads onto fewer physical servers and powers down the freed machines. The facility's measured total electricity draw falls, yet the reported PUE rises to 1.8. What best explains this?

opts.A: PUE is the ratio of total facility energy to IT-equipment energy, and much of the non-IT overhead (cooling plant, UPS losses, lighting) does not scale down with IT load, so shrinking the denominator raises the ratio even though total energy fell
opts.B: Servers that are powered down but still racked are reclassified from IT load into facility load, so they move into the numerator only
opts.C: Consolidation raises per-rack power density, and the additional cooling this demands always outweighs the energy saved by switching servers off
opts.D: PUE excludes virtualised servers from its IT-equipment term, so moving workloads onto hypervisors artificially shrinks the denominator

exp: PUE is total facility energy divided by IT energy, so it is an efficiency ratio and not a measure of absolute consumption; fixed overhead makes it worsen whenever IT load drops. Option C is tempting but is contradicted by the stem, which states total draw actually fell — this is why PUE alone is a poor sustainability target and is paired with absolute energy and carbon metrics.

sub: Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
q: A sustainability team wants to account for the greenhouse-gas emissions produced by mining, manufacturing and shipping the servers it buys, as distinct from the emissions of the electricity those servers draw while running. It notes that stretching the hardware refresh cycle from three years to five reduces this quantity per year of service. Which term names it?

opts.A: Operational carbon
opts.B: Embodied carbon
opts.C: Carbon Usage Effectiveness (CUE)
opts.D: Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE)

exp: Embodied (or embedded) carbon is the emissions locked into a device before it is ever switched on, which is why longer refresh cycles amortise it over more service years. Carbon Usage Effectiveness is the closest trap: it is total CO2e from facility energy divided by IT energy, so it measures operational emissions, not manufacturing ones.

sub: Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
q: A Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler (autoscaling/v2) is configured with minReplicas: 2, maxReplicas: 10, and a single Resource metric on cpu with target type Utilization and averageUtilization: 50. The Deployment is currently running 4 pods, and each pod is averaging 100% of its requested CPU. Ignoring stabilisation windows and scaling policies, what replica count does the HPA compute?
exp: The HPA applies desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue), which here is ceil(4 x 100 / 50) = 8, comfortably under maxReplicas. Option D assumes a breach of the target jumps straight to the maximum, and option A assumes the controller adds one replica per reconcile loop; neither reflects how the ratio-based algorithm works.

sub: Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
q: A pool of identically sized backend instances serves a mix of sub-10 ms API calls and occasional multi-second report generations. Under plain round-robin distribution, a few instances are saturated with long requests while others sit nearly idle. Assuming the load balancer can observe how many requests it currently has in flight to each backend, which algorithm most directly corrects this?

opts.A: Weighted round robin, with weights assigned in proportion to each instance's size
opts.B: Source-IP hashing, so each client is pinned to one backend
opts.C: Uniformly random backend selection on every request
opts.D: Least outstanding requests (least connections), sending each new request to the backend with the fewest in-flight requests

exp: Least-outstanding-requests is the standard remedy for highly variable request cost because it reacts to live occupancy rather than to position in a rotation. Weighted round robin is the tempting alternative but its weights are static and reflect capacity, not the current backlog, so an instance stuck on a long report keeps receiving its share.

sub: Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
q: A five-node consensus-based datastore that commits writes on a majority quorum is deployed across two availability zones: three nodes in AZ-a and two in AZ-b. AZ-a becomes unreachable. What happens to the cluster?

opts.A: The two surviving nodes cannot form a majority of the five configured members, so the cluster loses quorum and refuses writes until AZ-a returns or the membership is changed by an operator
opts.B: The two surviving nodes elect a leader among themselves and continue accepting writes at reduced throughput
opts.C: Quorum is automatically recalculated against the reachable membership, so two out of two becomes the new majority and service continues
opts.D: Writes continue to be accepted and are reconciled by last-write-wins once AZ-a rejoins

exp: A majority quorum is computed against the configured membership of five, so three nodes are required and the surviving two are stranded — which is precisely why quorum systems are spread across three availability zones rather than two. Option C is the most seductive, but automatic shrinking of the quorum on partition is exactly what would allow both sides to accept conflicting writes, so consensus protocols require an explicit operator-driven membership change instead.

sub: Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
q: During every rolling deployment behind a cloud load balancer, a small number of users see connections reset mid-request, even though replacement instances pass their health checks before the old instances are taken out of service. Which load-balancer setting addresses this most directly?

opts.A: Lengthening the health-check interval so instances are probed less aggressively
opts.B: Connection draining (deregistration delay), which stops new requests to a departing instance but lets in-flight requests finish within a grace period
opts.C: Enabling sticky sessions so each client stays bound to one instance
opts.D: Raising the load balancer's idle timeout for keep-alive connections

exp: Without a deregistration delay, an instance is removed from rotation and terminated while requests already dispatched to it are still executing, which the client observes as a reset. Sticky sessions are the tempting choice because they also concern client-to-instance binding, but they make the problem worse — a pinned client is guaranteed to be affected when its instance goes away.

sub: Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
q: Service A calls service B synchronously. B's p99 latency rises from 40 ms to 20 seconds. A's request-handling threads all end up blocked waiting on B, and A starts failing requests on endpoints that never touch B at all. Which resilience mechanism is specifically designed to stop A from continuing to issue calls to a dependency that is already failing?

opts.A: Automatic retries with exponential backoff and jitter on every call to B
opts.B: Horizontally autoscaling service A on average CPU utilisation
opts.C: A circuit breaker that opens after a failure or slow-call threshold is crossed and fails calls to B immediately while open
opts.D: Increasing A's client-side timeout for B so that slow responses are not abandoned

exp: A circuit breaker trips on observed failure or slow-call rate and then fails fast, freeing A's threads instead of parking them on a dependency that cannot answer. Retries with backoff and jitter are the trap: they are good practice for transient errors but here they multiply load against an already-overloaded B and hold A's threads even longer, and autoscaling A on CPU will not even fire, since threads blocked on I/O consume almost no CPU.

sub: Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
q: A cluster runs an API gateway at its edge and a service mesh internally. Which responsibility properly belongs to the API gateway rather than to the service mesh?

opts.A: Terminating mutual TLS on a call from one internal service to another
opts.B: Retrying an idempotent internal call against a second replica after the first returns 503
opts.C: Propagating trace-context headers across internal service-to-service hops
opts.D: Authenticating external third-party consumers by API key and enforcing a per-consumer request quota on traffic entering the cluster from the public internet

exp: The gateway owns north-south traffic — the boundary where untrusted external clients are identified, monetised and rate-limited per consumer — while the mesh owns east-west traffic between services that are already inside the trust boundary. The other three options all describe internal hops, which are exactly the sidecar's job in a mesh.

sub: Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
q: A cloud provider offers carbon-aware scheduling for deferrable batch workloads such as nightly model retraining. What does such a scheduler actually exploit in order to reduce emissions?

opts.A: It reduces the total kilowatt-hours the job consumes by compressing the same work into a shorter wall-clock window
opts.B: The carbon intensity of grid electricity (grams of CO2e per kWh) varies by hour and by region, so a job with a flexible deadline can be run at a time, or in a region, where the electricity is cleaner
opts.C: It retires renewable-energy certificates after the run so that the job's reported emissions net out to zero
opts.D: It restricts scheduling to providers that have published a net-zero commitment for the calendar year

exp: Carbon-aware scheduling is temporal and spatial shifting: the same kilowatt-hours are moved to a window or region where the marginal generation mix is less carbon-intense, which is why it only works for workloads with slack in their deadline. Option C describes offsetting, an accounting step applied after consumption that changes no scheduling decision at all.

sub: Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization
q: On 32-bit x86 before Intel VT-x and AMD-V, a hypervisor could not run a guest kernel by pure trap-and-emulate. Which property of that instruction set was the obstacle?

opts.A: The architecture offered only two usable privilege levels, leaving no ring in which a guest kernel could sit between applications and the hypervisor
opts.B: Instructions were variable-length, so the hypervisor could not decode the guest instruction stream quickly enough to emulate it in software
opts.C: Several sensitive instructions were not privileged: executed from user mode they quietly returned host state or ignored the operation instead of faulting to the hypervisor
opts.D: The MMU exposed host physical addresses to ring 3, so any guest could read memory frames belonging to a co-resident guest

exp: Popek and Goldberg's condition for classical virtualisability is that every sensitive instruction also be privileged, and x86 broke it: instructions such as PUSHF/POPF and the store-descriptor-table family execute in user mode without trapping, so the hypervisor never gains control to emulate them. Ring count was never the problem — x86 has four rings, and VMware's answer was binary translation of the offending instructions, not extra rings.

sub: Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization
q: Compared with the binary-translation approach of early x86 hypervisors, what does hardware-assisted virtualisation (Intel VT-x / AMD-V) actually add to the processor?

opts.A: A second, orthogonal execution mode: the guest runs in non-root mode at its own normal privilege level, and configured sensitive events cause a VM exit into root mode where the hypervisor handles them
opts.B: A hardware rewriting engine that converts guest kernel instructions into safe host instructions, taking over the job of the hypervisor's software translation cache
opts.C: A firmware-reserved physical core on which all of a guest's privileged instructions are executed in isolation from the rest of the host
opts.D: An extra privilege ring below ring 0 into which the guest kernel is deprivileged, so that every ring-0 instruction it issues faults in the normal way

exp: VT-x and AMD-V introduce root and non-root operation with guest state held in a hardware control structure (VMCS on Intel, VMCB on AMD): the guest kernel keeps running at ring 0 inside non-root mode and leaves via VM exits, so no instruction rewriting is required. The popular 'ring -1' phrasing behind option D is loose — it is the hypervisor that moves into a separate mode, not the guest that is pushed into a new ring.

sub: Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization
q: A hypervisor moves from software-maintained shadow page tables to hardware nested paging (Intel EPT / AMD RVI). What is the essential trade-off of that move?

opts.A: It removes the memory overhead of the shadow tables, but requires the guest kernel to be modified so that every page-table update becomes an explicit hypercall
opts.B: It removes the host's dependence on an IOMMU, but in exchange no physical device can any longer be assigned directly to a guest
opts.C: It eliminates the guest's own page tables entirely, but the hypervisor must then service every page fault the guest takes
opts.D: It removes the VM exits previously needed to keep shadow tables synchronised with guest page-table edits, but a TLB miss now costs a two-dimensional walk through both guest and nested tables

exp: Nested paging lets the CPU walk the guest and host translations itself, so the guest may edit its own page tables freely and the exit-heavy shadow-table maintenance disappears, at the cost of a far longer walk on each TLB miss — which is exactly why large pages matter more under EPT/RVI. Option A describes a paravirtualised MMU, a different technique in which the guest is modified; nested paging needs no guest changes at all.

sub: Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization
q: A host is short of physical memory, so the hypervisor inflates the balloon driver running inside one of its guests. What does inflating the balloon accomplish?

opts.A: It compresses the guest's least-recently-used pages into a host-side compression cache so that reclaiming them does not require disk I/O
opts.B: It allocates and pins pages inside the guest, letting the guest's own memory manager choose which pages to surrender, after which the hypervisor reclaims the host frames backing them
opts.C: It scans co-resident VMs for pages with identical contents and maps them onto a single shared host frame, freeing the duplicates
opts.D: It writes the guest's pages out to the host's swap file without the guest's participation and entirely transparently to the guest OS

exp: Ballooning is deliberately cooperative: the in-guest driver demands memory, and because the guest OS picks the victims it gives up the pages it considers least valuable, which is far better than the host guessing blindly. Option D is host swapping — the uncooperative fallback used when ballooning cannot reclaim fast enough — while C is transparent page sharing and A is memory compression, both separate reclamation techniques.

sub: Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization
q: On a contended VMware vSphere cluster, a VM configured with 16 vCPUs performs worse than the same VM did with 8 vCPUs. The application is heavily multithreaded and keeps nearly all of its vCPUs busy, and the host's physical cores are oversubscribed across many VMs. What best explains this?

opts.A: The VM's vCPUs must progress within a bounded skew of one another, so a vCPU that runs ahead is co-stopped until its lagging siblings can be scheduled alongside it, which on a contended host shows up as co-stop time (%CSTP)
opts.B: Each extra vCPU reserves a fixed slice of host RAM for its register save area, leaving the guest with markedly less memory for its page cache
opts.C: The hypervisor pins each vCPU to a dedicated physical core, so a 16-vCPU VM cannot be scheduled at all unless 16 cores are permanently idle
opts.D: The guest scheduler keeps migrating threads across all 16 vCPUs, and each such migration forces a VM exit into the hypervisor

exp: ESXi uses relaxed co-scheduling: it tracks how far each vCPU has fallen behind its siblings and co-starts the skewed ones together, so a wide VM on an oversubscribed host repeatedly waits for enough physical cores to free up at the same moment. The documented signature is co-stop time, %CSTP, and it is distinct from %RDY: %RDY counts time a vCPU was ready to run with no physical CPU available, whereas %CSTP counts time lost specifically to co-scheduling skew, which is the counter VMware's right-sizing guidance says to watch. Relaxed co-scheduling deliberately does not penalise idle vCPUs — a halted vCPU accrues no skew — so this bites a genuinely busy wide VM rather than a mostly idle one. Option C overstates the mechanism: vCPUs are time-shared against physical cores, not permanently pinned to them.
reviewFix: Stem, key option and explanation all corrected; keyed letter A unchanged. Both blind passes flagged this, and their two findings compounded. First, the old stem stipulated that only four threads were ever busy and guest CPU utilisation stayed low — which is precisely the workload relaxed co-scheduling was designed NOT to penalise, since a descheduled idle vCPU accrues no skew, so the question asserted a co-start stall in the one case ESXi exempts. The stem now has the guest actually keeping its vCPUs busy, which makes co-scheduling the honest explanation. Second, the option and explanation diagnosed it with the wrong counter: %RDY is time a vCPU was ready with no physical CPU free, while %CSTP (co-stop) is the documented signature of an oversized vSMP VM and the one right-sizing guidance tells you to watch. Both now say %CSTP, and the explanation states the idle-vCPU exemption explicitly so the rule is not over-generalised.

sub: Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization
q: A tenant VM needs near-line-rate throughput from a shared 25 GbE NIC with minimal host CPU cost, so the operator enables SR-IOV on that NIC and assigns the VM a virtual function. What has changed for that VM's traffic?

opts.A: The hypervisor's software switch is given exclusive use of a physical core, so its packet-processing loop is no longer preempted by guest vCPUs
opts.B: The emulated NIC in the guest is replaced by a paravirtualised device whose driver shares a descriptor ring with the host, halving the number of packet copies
opts.C: The entire NIC port is handed to the VM through the IOMMU, so that VM has sole use of the port and every other VM must be placed on a different port
opts.D: The NIC presents itself as several lightweight PCIe functions; one is assigned directly to the VM, which drives it with its own driver and DMAs into guest memory, bypassing the hypervisor's software switch

exp: SR-IOV splits one physical function into many virtual functions that the NIC switches between in hardware, so each VM owns a VF directly while the IOMMU confines that VF's DMA to the owning guest's memory. Option C describes plain PCI passthrough, which cannot scale beyond the number of physical ports, and option B describes a paravirtualised device such as virtio-net, whose packets still traverse the host.

sub: Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization
q:
On a KVM host, `qemu-img info` reports the following for a VM's disk image:
  file format: qcow2
  virtual size: 40 GiB
  disk size: 1.31 GiB
  backing file: golden-base.qcow2
Which statement about this disk is correct?

opts.A: The 40 GiB figure is an upper quota only; the guest currently sees just 1.31 GiB of usable disk until the image is explicitly resized
opts.B: It is a copy-on-write overlay: only blocks written since it was created are stored here, every untouched block is read from golden-base.qcow2, which must remain present and unmodified
opts.C: golden-base.qcow2 is an incremental backup written after each shutdown of this VM, and may safely be deleted once the VM has booted cleanly
opts.D: The image is a compressed full clone in which 1.31 GiB holds the compressed form of the 40 GiB volume, and the base image is no longer referenced at runtime

exp: A backing file makes the image an overlay: any cluster the overlay has never written is read through to the base, so deleting or editing golden-base.qcow2 corrupts every overlay built on it — this is precisely how golden images and linked clones are implemented. The guest still sees the full 40 GiB; `disk size` merely reports how much of the host's storage the sparse overlay occupies today, which is why option A misreads the two figures.

sub: Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization
q: A guest deletes 200 GB of files from a thin-provisioned virtual disk on a SAN-backed datastore. Free space inside the guest filesystem rises at once, but consumed capacity on the datastore and on the array does not fall. What explains this, and what brings the space back?

opts.A: The array is holding the freed blocks in its write cache; consumed capacity will drop of its own accord once that cache destages to disk
opts.B: Consumed capacity is recomputed only when a snapshot is taken, so the figure will correct itself at the next scheduled snapshot of the VM
opts.C: Deleting a file only rewrites guest filesystem metadata, so the underlying blocks stay allocated until the guest issues SCSI UNMAP / TRIM and the virtualisation and storage stack passes that reclamation down to the array
opts.D: For a thin-provisioned disk the datastore always displays the provisioned size rather than actual usage, so the figure shown was never going to change

exp: A delete is a metadata operation inside the guest filesystem, so the hypervisor and the array still believe those blocks are in use; reclamation requires an UNMAP/TRIM hint propagated from the guest filesystem through the virtual disk down to the array, which is why guests are mounted with discard support or run a periodic trim. Option D is the reverse of how thin provisioning is reported — the whole point of a thin datastore is that it reports blocks actually allocated, not the provisioned size.

sub: Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization
q: A write-heavy in-memory database VM is being live-migrated between two hosts that use shared storage. The hypervisor copies its memory, then copies more memory, and after several passes the migration is abandoned instead of completing. What is happening?

opts.A: The destination host reports a different CPU model, so each page must be re-encoded for that model before the destination will accept it
opts.B: Because storage is shared, the virtual disk is transferred alongside memory on every pass, and the disk is far larger than the VM's RAM
opts.C: Pre-copy migration re-sends the pages dirtied during the previous pass; this workload dirties memory faster than the migration link can ship it, so the residual set never shrinks enough to enter the brief stop-and-copy phase
opts.D: Every pass retransmits the guest's entire memory from the beginning, so the total transfer time is fixed and simply exceeds the configured migration timeout

exp: Pre-copy converges only while the guest's page dirty rate stays below the achievable transfer rate; a write-heavy in-memory workload can outrun the link, leaving a large residual working set and forcing the hypervisor to give up — the usual remedies are a faster migration network, throttling the vCPUs, or a post-copy strategy that resumes on the destination and faults pages across. Option B inverts the purpose of shared storage: the disk is not copied at all, only memory and device state are.

sub: Containers, Docker, Kubernetes orchestration, Infrastructure as Code and DevOps
q: A team runs a sharded datastore on Kubernetes. Each replica needs a hostname that stays the same across rescheduling, and its own PersistentVolume that is re-attached to that same replica rather than to whichever Pod starts first. Which workload object provides this?

opts.A: A Deployment whose Pod template mounts a PersistentVolumeClaim
opts.B: A DaemonSet, so that each replica is pinned to one node
opts.C: A StatefulSet with a volumeClaimTemplate
opts.D: A ReplicaSet with pod anti-affinity across nodes

exp: A StatefulSet gives every Pod a stable ordinal identity and name, and its volumeClaimTemplate creates a separate PersistentVolumeClaim per ordinal that is rebound to the same ordinal whenever that Pod is recreated. A Deployment mounting a PersistentVolumeClaim (A) points every replica at the one same claim and hands out randomised Pod names, so neither the identity nor the per-replica volume requirement is met.

sub: Containers, Docker, Kubernetes orchestration, Infrastructure as Code and DevOps
q: Which Service configuration makes cluster DNS resolve the Service name to the individual Pod IP addresses of its ready endpoints, instead of to one virtual IP that load-balances across them?

opts.A: Setting clusterIP: None, i.e. a headless Service
opts.B: type: NodePort
opts.C: type: ExternalName
opts.D: type: LoadBalancer with externalTrafficPolicy: Local

exp: A headless Service is allocated no virtual IP, so the cluster DNS server answers the Service name with one address record per ready endpoint — the mechanism StatefulSet members use to find their peers directly. ExternalName is the other DNS-special Service type but it returns a CNAME to a name outside the cluster and has no endpoints at all.

sub: Containers, Docker, Kubernetes orchestration, Infrastructure as Code and DevOps
q: A container's readiness probe starts failing while its liveness probe keeps succeeding. What does Kubernetes do?

opts.A: The kubelet restarts the container once the readiness probe's failureThreshold is reached
opts.B: The Pod is evicted and rescheduled onto a different node
opts.C: Nothing changes for that Pod until the liveness probe also begins to fail
opts.D: The Pod's address is removed from the Service's endpoints, but the container is left running

exp: Readiness controls endpoint membership only: a Pod that reports not-ready is dropped from the Service's endpoints so it stops receiving traffic, while its container continues to run untouched. Restarting a container is strictly the liveness probe's job, which is why C is wrong — the Pod's traffic does change immediately, even though nothing restarts.

sub: Containers, Docker, Kubernetes orchestration, Infrastructure as Code and DevOps
q:
A Dockerfile contains:

FROM debian:stable-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y gcc
RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY ./src /src

The image is built normally, with no multi-stage build and no squashing. What is the effect of the third instruction on the size of the resulting image?

opts.A: The image shrinks by roughly the size of the deleted package lists
opts.B: The image does not shrink; the files stay in the earlier layer and the new layer only records their deletion
opts.C: The build fails, because a RUN instruction cannot delete files created by a previous RUN instruction
opts.D: The image shrinks only because the deletion happens before the final COPY instruction

exp: Image layers are additive and immutable: deleting a file in a later layer writes a whiteout entry that hides it from the assembled filesystem, but the earlier layer still ships the bytes, so the sum of the layers is unchanged. To actually reclaim the space the cleanup must run inside the same RUN instruction that created the files, or the wanted artefacts must be copied into a fresh stage.

sub: Containers, Docker, Kubernetes orchestration, Infrastructure as Code and DevOps
q: With default options, what does `terraform plan` compare in order to produce the diff it prints?

opts.A: The configuration against state that has first been refreshed from the providers' real remote objects, making no changes of its own
opts.B: The configuration against the state file exactly as stored, without contacting any provider API
opts.C: The current configuration against the previous revision of the configuration in version control
opts.D: The state file against the dependency lock file that pins provider versions
